questions.question: For 4.4 g of carbon dioxide (C = 12, O = 16; N_A = 6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹), what are the number of molecules, the total number of atoms, the total number of electrons, and the mass of one molecule?
options: A) 6.022 × 10²² molecules; 1.807 × 10²³ atoms; 1.325 × 10²⁴ electrons; 7.31 × 10⁻²³ g
B) 6.022 × 10²³ molecules; 1.807 × 10²⁴ atoms; 1.325 × 10²⁵ electrons; 44 g
C) 6.022 × 10²² molecules; 6.022 × 10²² atoms; 1.325 × 10²³ electrons; 7.31 × 10⁻²² g
D) 1.0 × 10²² molecules; 3.0 × 10²² atoms; 2.2 × 10²³ electrons; 4.4 × 10⁻²³ g
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 6.022 × 10²² molecules; 1.807 × 10²³ atoms; 1.325 × 10²⁴ electrons; 7.31 × 10⁻²³ g.
Concept: One mole of any substance contains Avogadro's number (6.022 × 10²³) of elementary entities (atoms, molecules, ions). The molar mass in grams is numerically equal to the atomic, molecular or formula mass in u. The structure of a molecule tells how many atoms and electrons each molecule contains.
Given: m = 4.4 g; M(CO₂) = 12 + 2 × 16 = 44 g mol⁻¹; each CO₂ has 3 atoms and 6 + 2 × 8 = 22 electrons.
Formula/Principle: n = m/M; N = nN_A; mass of one molecule = M/N_A.
Step 1: n = 4.4 ÷ 44 = 0.10 mol; molecules = 0.10 × 6.022 × 10²³ = 6.022 × 10²².
Step 2: Atoms = 3 × 6.022 × 10²² = 1.807 × 10²³; electrons = 22 × 6.022 × 10²² = 1.325 × 10²⁴.
Step 3: Mass of one molecule = 44 ÷ 6.022 × 10²³ = 7.31 × 10⁻²³ g.
Why: Each molecule is one entity counted by the mole, and its formula (one C and two O atoms, 22 electrons) converts molecule counts into atom and electron counts.
Why not the others: (B) Treats 4.4 g as 1 mol, and 44 g is the molar mass, not the mass of one molecule. (C) Forgets that each molecule has three atoms, and the electron count and molecular mass are off by a factor of 10. (D) Uses the wrong Avogadro number.
Key point: n = m/M; multiply by N_A for entities, and by atoms or electrons per molecule for those counts.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Ranking distances of closest approach for alpha particles hitting gold and silver nuclei at different energies, and why the Thomson model fails
questions.question: In Rutherford-type scattering, α-particles approach nuclei head-on. Rank the distances of closest approach for: P — 5.0 MeV α-particles on gold (Z = 79); Q — 5.0 MeV α-particles on silver (Z = 47); R — 10.0 MeV α-particles on gold (take e²/(4πε₀) = 1.44 MeV fm). Which statement about atomic models is also correct?
options: A) R > P > Q; in the Thomson model, the positive charge is concentrated in a tiny nucleus
B) P = Q = R; closest approach depends only on the nucleus
C) Q > P > R; most α-particles were deflected through large angles

D) P (about 45 fm) > Q (about 27 fm) > R (about 23 fm); in Thomson's model, positive charge is spread uniformly over the whole atom, so it cannot deflect α-particles strongly, whereas the observed backscattering of a very few α-particles requires a small, dense, positively charged nucleus
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) P ≈ 45 fm > Q ≈ 27 fm > R ≈ 23 fm; Thomson's spread-out positive charge cannot explain large deflections.
Concept: Thomson proposed that an atom is a sphere of positive charge with electrons embedded in it (plum pudding or watermelon model). Rutherford's α-particle scattering experiment showed that most α-particles passed undeflected, a small fraction were deflected by small angles, and a very few (about 1 in 20 000) bounced back. He concluded that most of the space in an atom is empty and that the positive charge and most of the mass are concentrated in a very small nucleus. At the distance of closest approach in a head-on collision, all the kinetic energy has become electrostatic potential energy.
Given: K = 5.0 or 10.0 MeV; Z = 79 or 47; α charge = 2e.
Formula/Principle: K = (1/4πε₀)(2e)(Ze)/r₀ ⇒ r₀ = 2Z × 1.44 MeV fm ÷ K.
Step 1: P: r₀ = 2 × 79 × 1.44 ÷ 5.0 = 45.5 fm.
Step 2: Q: r₀ = 2 × 47 × 1.44 ÷ 5.0 = 27.1 fm.
Step 3: R: r₀ = 2 × 79 × 1.44 ÷ 10.0 = 22.8 fm.
Why: r₀ ∝ Z/K: a larger nuclear charge repels more strongly (larger r₀), and a more energetic α-particle gets closer (smaller r₀). Even 23 fm is larger than the gold nucleus (about 7 fm), so the scattering is purely electrostatic. A diffuse positive charge would produce only weak forces and small deflections.
Why not the others: (A) Doubling the energy halves r₀, so R is the smallest; Thomson's model has no nucleus. (B) r₀ depends on the energy and the charge. (C) Silver has a smaller Z, so Q < P; only a very few α-particles were strongly deflected.
Key point: r₀ = 2Ze²/(4πε₀K) ∝ Z/K; large-angle scattering shows a tiny dense nucleus.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Classification of Elements and Periodicity; s and p block trends
questions.sub_topic: Reading successive ionisation enthalpies to find the group of an element, and explaining the Be > B and N > O anomalies
questions.question: The first four ionisation enthalpies of element X are 738, 1451, 7733 and 10 540 kJ mol⁻¹. Which conclusion is correct?
options: A) X has three valence electrons and belongs to group 13

B) X has two valence electrons and belongs to group 2, forming X²⁺, since the very large jump comes after the second electron; for a similar reason of electron arrangement, the first ionisation enthalpy of boron is lower than that of beryllium, because the 2p electron of boron is shielded by the 2s electrons and is easier to remove, and that of oxygen is lower than that of nitrogen, because oxygen's fourth 2p electron is paired
C) X has one valence electron, because the first ionisation enthalpy is the smallest
D) X belongs to group 18, because its ionisation enthalpies are large
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Two valence electrons (group 2, forms X²⁺); B < Be and O < N explained by shielding and pairing.
Concept: Successive ionisation enthalpies always increase, because each electron is removed from an increasingly positive ion, but a very large jump occurs when an electron must be removed from a complete inner (noble-gas) shell. Thus the position of the large jump reveals the number of valence electrons. The first ionisation enthalpy of boron is smaller than that of beryllium, because the 2s electrons shield the 2p electron of boron from the nucleus more than 2s electrons shield each other; that of oxygen is smaller than that of nitrogen, because in oxygen two of the four 2p electrons occupy the same orbital, and their repulsion makes one of them easier to remove.
Why: The ratio IE₂/IE₁ ≈ 2, a normal increase, but IE₃/IE₂ ≈ 5.3, a huge jump. After two electrons are removed, X²⁺ has a noble-gas core, so the third electron comes from an inner shell. The data fit magnesium.
Why not the others: (A) The large jump would then come after the third electron. (C) The jump would come after the first electron. (D) A noble gas has a very high first ionisation enthalpy, and 738 kJ mol⁻¹ is low.
Key point: The big jump in successive IEs marks the end of the valence electrons (here after 2 → group 2).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Shapes of I3−, ICl4− and PCl5 by VSEPR, unequal axial and equatorial bonds in PCl5, and bond angles in NH4+, NH3 and H2O
questions.question: Which statement is correct according to VSEPR theory?
options: A) I₃⁻ is bent, because the central iodine has lone pairs; ICl₄⁻ is tetrahedral; PCl₅ has five identical P–Cl bonds
B) ICl₄⁻ is tetrahedral like NH₄⁺, and the bond angle of H₂O is larger than that of NH₃

C) I₃⁻ (two bond pairs and three lone pairs on the central atom) is linear; ICl₄⁻ (four bond pairs and two lone pairs) is square planar; in trigonal bipyramidal PCl₅ the two axial bonds are longer than the three equatorial bonds, because axial bond pairs suffer more repulsion from equatorial bond pairs; and the bond angles decrease NH₄⁺ (109.5°) > NH₃ (107°) > H₂O (104.5°) as the number of lone pairs increases
D) PCl₅ is square pyramidal, and its equatorial bonds are longer than its axial bonds
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) I₃⁻ linear; ICl₄⁻ square planar; PCl₅ axial bonds longer; angles NH₄⁺ > NH₃ > H₂O.
Concept: The shape of a molecule depends on the number of valence-shell electron pairs (bonded or non-bonded) around the central atom. Electron pairs repel one another and take up positions that minimise repulsion. The repulsive interactions decrease in the order lone pair–lone pair > lone pair–bond pair > bond pair–bond pair. Lone pairs occupy positions that reduce lone pair–lone pair repulsion: in a trigonal bipyramid, they go to the equatorial positions; in an octahedron, they go opposite each other. In PCl₅, each axial bond pair experiences more repulsion from the equatorial bond pairs, so the axial bonds are slightly longer (and weaker).
Why: I₃⁻: five electron pairs (trigonal bipyramidal arrangement); the three lone pairs occupy the equatorial positions, leaving the two bonds axial and collinear. ICl₄⁻: six pairs (octahedral arrangement); the two lone pairs sit opposite each other, leaving four bonds in a square. NH₄⁺, NH₃ and H₂O all have four electron pairs, but 0, 1 and 2 lone pairs compress the bond angle progressively.
Why not the others: (A) I₃⁻ is linear, ICl₄⁻ is square planar, and PCl₅'s bonds are not identical. (B) ICl₄⁻ has six electron pairs, and H₂O has a smaller angle than NH₃. (D) PCl₅ is trigonal bipyramidal, with longer axial bonds.
Key point: Lone pairs: equatorial in a trigonal bipyramid, trans in an octahedron; lp–lp > lp–bp > bp–bp.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Calculating and ranking entropy changes for vaporisation, fusion and the formation of liquid water, with the second-law criterion
questions.question: The enthalpy of vaporisation of water at 373 K is 40.79 kJ mol⁻¹, and its enthalpy of fusion at 273 K is 6.01 kJ mol⁻¹. Rank the entropy changes of these processes: P — vaporisation of 1 mol water at 373 K; Q — melting of 1 mol ice at 273 K; R — 2H₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2H₂O(l) at 298 K. Which statement is also correct?
options: A) Q > P > R; the entropy of an isolated system always decreases in a spontaneous process
B) R > P > Q; the entropy of a system always increases in every spontaneous process
C) P = Q > R; entropy changes do not depend on the physical state

D) P (about +109 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹) > Q (about +22 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹) > R (negative); for a spontaneous process, the total entropy change of the system and its surroundings is positive, so R, with a negative ΔS for the system, proceeds because it releases heat that increases the entropy of the surroundings
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) ΔS(P) ≈ +109 > ΔS(Q) ≈ +22 > ΔS(R) < 0 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹; total entropy increases in a spontaneous change.
Concept: Entropy is a measure of the degree of randomness or disorder in a system. For a reversible phase change at its transition temperature, ΔS = ΔH/T. Entropy increases from solid to liquid to gas, and a reaction that decreases the number of gas molecules has a negative entropy change. The second law of thermodynamics states that the total entropy change (system plus surroundings) is positive for a spontaneous process; at constant temperature and pressure this is expressed as ΔG = ΔH − TΔS < 0.
Given: ΔvapH = 40.79 kJ mol⁻¹ at 373 K; ΔfusH = 6.01 kJ mol⁻¹ at 273 K.
Formula/Principle: ΔS = ΔH/T for a reversible phase change.
Step 1: P: ΔS = 40 790 ÷ 373 ≈ +109 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.
Step 2: Q: ΔS = 6010 ÷ 273 ≈ +22.0 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.
Step 3: R: 3 mol of gas become 2 mol of liquid, a large decrease in disorder, so ΔS < 0.
Why: Turning a liquid into a gas creates far more disorder than melting a solid, because gas molecules move freely through a much larger volume. A process with ΔS(system) < 0 can still be spontaneous if it is exothermic enough to raise the entropy of the surroundings by more.
Why not the others: (A) Vaporisation increases entropy more than melting, and the entropy of an isolated system increases in a spontaneous process. (B) Formation of liquid water from gases decreases entropy; spontaneous processes can decrease the system's entropy. (C) The two phase changes have very different entropy changes.
Key point: ΔS_vap ≫ ΔS_fus > 0; gas → liquid ΔS < 0; spontaneity needs ΔS(total) > 0.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Matching measured pH values of 0.10 M salt solutions with salts that do or do not hydrolyse
questions.question: The pH values 7.00, 8.88, 5.12 and 7.00 are measured for 0.10 mol L⁻¹ solutions of four salts: NaCl, CH₃COONa, NH₄Cl and CH₃COONH₄ (pKₐ of acetic acid = 4.76; pK_b of ammonia = 4.75; 298 K). Which matching and reasoning are correct?
options: A) CH₃COONa has pH 8.88, because acetate hydrolyses to give OH⁻; NH₄Cl has pH 5.12, because NH₄⁺ hydrolyses to give H₃O⁺; NaCl has pH 7.00, because neither ion hydrolyses; and CH₃COONH₄ has pH close to 7.00, because both ions hydrolyse to similar extents (pKₐ ≈ pK_b), and its pH does not depend on concentration
B) CH₃COONa has pH 5.12, and NH₄Cl has pH 8.88
C) NaCl has pH 8.88, because Na⁺ hydrolyses
D) CH₃COONH₄ has pH 8.88, because acetate hydrolyses but ammonium does not
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) CH₃COONa 8.88, NH₄Cl 5.12, NaCl 7.00, CH₃COONH₄ ≈ 7.00.
Concept: Salts of strong acids and strong bases (NaCl) do not hydrolyse, and their solutions are neutral. Salts of weak acids and strong bases (CH₃COONa) are basic, because the anion hydrolyses: CH₃COO⁻ + H₂O ⇌ CH₃COOH + OH⁻. Salts of strong acids and weak bases (NH₄Cl) are acidic: NH₄⁺ + H₂O ⇌ NH₃ + H₃O⁺. For salts of a weak acid and a weak base, both ions hydrolyse, and pH = 7 + ½(pKₐ − pK_b), independent of concentration.
Given: c = 0.10 mol L⁻¹; pKₐ = 4.76; pK_b = 4.75.
Formula/Principle: Weak acid–strong base salt: pH = 7 + ½(pKₐ + log c). Strong acid–weak base salt: pH = 7 − ½(pK_b + log c). Weak–weak: pH = 7 + ½(pKₐ − pK_b).
Step 1: CH₃COONa: pH = 7 + ½(4.76 − 1) = 7 + 1.88 = 8.88.
Step 2: NH₄Cl: pH = 7 − ½(4.75 − 1) = 7 − 1.875 = 5.12 (to two decimals).
Step 3: CH₃COONH₄: pH = 7 + ½(4.76 − 4.75) = 7.005 ≈ 7.00.
Why: The ion derived from the weak partner reacts with water, generating OH⁻ or H₃O⁺; when both ions are from weak partners of nearly equal strength, their effects cancel.
Why not the others: (B) This swaps the acidic and basic salts. (C) Na⁺ comes from a strong base and does not hydrolyse. (D) In ammonium acetate, NH₄⁺ also hydrolyses, balancing the acetate.
Key point: Weak-acid salt → basic; weak-base salt → acidic; weak–weak salt → pH = 7 + ½(pKₐ − pK_b).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: pH of an ammonia–ammonium chloride buffer and its small change when a strong base is added
questions.question: A buffer contains 0.20 mol NH₃ and 0.10 mol NH₄Cl in 1.0 L (pK_b of NH₃ = 4.75; 298 K). What is its pH, and what is the pH after 0.020 mol of solid NaOH is dissolved in it (negligible volume change)?
options: C) 9.55, then 9.69; the added OH⁻ converts some NH₄⁺ to NH₃, so the ratio [NH₃]/[NH₄⁺] rises from 2.0 to 2.75 and the pH changes by only about 0.14
D) 9.55, then 9.55; a buffer's pH cannot change at all
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) pH 9.55, rising only to 9.69.
Concept: A buffer resists changes in pH on the addition of small amounts of acid or base. A basic buffer is a weak base with its conjugate acid (salt). For it, the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation gives pOH = pK_b + log([salt]/[base]), and pH = 14 − pOH at 298 K. Added OH⁻ reacts with the conjugate acid: NH₄⁺ + OH⁻ → NH₃ + H₂O.
Given: [NH₃] = 0.20 M; [NH₄⁺] = 0.10 M; pK_b = 4.75; added OH⁻ = 0.020 mol in 1.0 L.
Formula/Principle: pOH = pK_b + log([NH₄⁺]/[NH₃]); pH = 14 − pOH.
Step 1: pOH = 4.75 + log(0.10/0.20) = 4.75 − 0.301 = 4.45; pH = 9.55.
Step 2: After NaOH: [NH₄⁺] = 0.10 − 0.02 = 0.08 M; [NH₃] = 0.20 + 0.02 = 0.22 M.
Step 3: pOH = 4.75 + log(0.08/0.22) = 4.75 − 0.439 = 4.31; pH = 9.69.
Why: The buffer converts strong base into the weak base NH₃, so only the ratio of base to conjugate acid changes, and the pH depends on the logarithm of that ratio. The same 0.020 mol NaOH in 1 L of pure water would give pH = 14 − 1.70 = 12.30.
Why not the others: (A) 9.25 ignores the 2 : 1 ratio, and 12.30 is the value for pure water. (B) These are the pOH values, not pH. (D) A buffer reduces the change, but does not prevent it entirely.
Key point: Basic buffer: pOH = pK_b + log([salt]/[base]); added OH⁻ shifts the ratio slightly.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Oxidation numbers in compounds with peroxide, superoxide and oxygen–fluorine bonds, where simple rules mislead
questions.question: Which set gives the correct oxidation numbers of the stated atoms: Cr in CrO₅ (one oxo oxygen and two peroxo groups), S in H₂SO₅ (peroxomonosulfuric acid, one peroxo group), O in KO₂, and O in OF₂?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Cr +6, S +6, O −½ (superoxide), O +2 (in OF₂).
Concept: Oxygen usually has an oxidation number of −2, but in peroxides (O₂²⁻) each oxygen is −1, in superoxides (O₂⁻) each is −½, and when bonded to fluorine (OF₂, O₂F₂) it is positive (+2 or +1), because fluorine, the most electronegative element, is always −1. An oxidation number calculated by assuming all oxygens are −2 can exceed the group maximum, which shows that peroxo linkages are present.
Given: CrO₅ = 1 O²⁻ + 2 O₂²⁻; H₂SO₅ has one –O–O– group; KO₂ has O₂⁻; OF₂ has F at −1.
Formula/Principle: The sum of oxidation numbers equals the charge on the species.
Step 1: CrO₅: x + (−2) + 4(−1) = 0 ⇒ x = +6 (taking all O as −2 would give +10, impossible for group 6).
Step 2: H₂SO₅: 2(+1) + x + 3(−2) + 2(−1) = 0 ⇒ x = +6 (all O as −2 would give +8).
Step 3: KO₂: +1 + 2y = 0 ⇒ y = −½. OF₂: z + 2(−1) = 0 ⇒ z = +2.
Why: Oxidation numbers must respect the bonding: a peroxo O–O bond contributes nothing to oxygen's oxidation number, so each peroxo oxygen is −1. The maximum oxidation state of Cr or S is +6 (the group number for groups 6 and 16), which confirms the answers.
Why not the others: (A) Treats every oxygen as −2, giving impossible +10 and +8 values. (C) Ignores the peroxo group in H₂SO₅, uses the peroxide value for superoxide, and ignores fluorine's −1. (D) Miscounts the peroxo oxygens in CrO₅ and misses the superoxide.
Key point: Peroxide O −1, superoxide O −½, O in OF₂ +2; results above the group maximum signal peroxo bonds.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: The point on the x-axis equidistant from two given points, and why it lies on the perpendicular bisector plane of the segment
questions.question: Which point \(P\) on the \(x\)-axis is equidistant from \(A(1,2,3)\) and \(B(3,5,-2)\)? What is \(PA\), and how is \(P\) related to the midpoint \(M\) of \(AB\)?
options: A) \(P(2,0,0)\); \(PA=\sqrt{14}\); \(P\) coincides with \(M\)
B) \(P(-6,0,0)\); \(PA=\sqrt{62}\); \(PM\) is parallel to \(AB\)
C) \(P(4,0,0)\); \(PA=\sqrt{22}\); \(P\) lies on the line \(AB\)
D) \(P(6,0,0)\); \(PA=\sqrt{38}\); \(\vec{PM}\) is perpendicular to \(\vec{AB}\), since every point equidistant from \(A\) and \(B\) lies on the plane that bisects \(AB\) at right angles
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(P(6,0,0)\); \(PA=\sqrt{38}\); \(PM\perp AB\).
Given: \(A(1,2,3),\ B(3,5,-2);\ P=(x,0,0)\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{distance }=\sqrt{(x_2-x_1)^2+(y_2-y_1)^2+(z_2-z_1)^2};\ \text{midpoint }=\left(\tfrac{x_1+x_2}2,\tfrac{y_1+y_2}2,\tfrac{z_1+z_2}2\right)\)
Step 1: \(PA^2=PB^2:\ (x-1)^2+4+9=(x-3)^2+25+4\Rightarrow-2x+14=-6x+38\Rightarrow x=6\)
Step 2: \(PA=\sqrt{25+4+9}=\sqrt{38};\ PB=\sqrt{9+25+4}=\sqrt{38}\ \checkmark\)
Step 3: \(M=\left(2,\tfrac72,\tfrac12\right),\ \vec{PM}=\left(-4,\tfrac72,\tfrac12\right),\ \vec{AB}=(2,3,-5)\)
Worked derivation: \[\vec{PM}\cdot\vec{AB}=-8+\tfrac{21}2-\tfrac52=0\Rightarrow PM\perp AB\]
Check: \[\text{the triangle PAB is isosceles }(PA=PB)\text{, so the median from P is also the altitude}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the set of points equidistant from A and B is the perpendicular bisector plane of AB; P is where the x-axis meets that plane}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(M=(2,3.5,0.5)\text{ is not on the x-axis, and }(2,0,0)\text{ is not equidistant}\); (B) \(\text{sign slip in solving}\); (C) \((4,0,0)\text{ gives }PA^2=22,\ PB^2=30\).
Key point: \(PA=PB\iff P\text{ lies on the perpendicular bisector plane of AB}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Recovering a set A from two elements of A × A, counting relations on A, and reading a relation as points on a grid
questions.question: The Cartesian product \(A\times A\) has 16 elements, among which are \((-1,2)\) and \((0,3)\). What is \(A\), how many relations on \(A\) are there, and what are the domain and range of \(R=\{(x,y)\in A\times A:\ y=x+3\}\)?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(A=\{-1,0,2,3\}\); \(2^{16}\) relations; domain \(\{-1,0\}\), range \(\{2,3\}\).
Given: \(|A\times A|=16\Rightarrow|A|=4;\ (-1,2),(0,3)\in A\times A\)
Formula/Principle: \((a,b)\in A\times A\Rightarrow a,b\in A;\ \text{relations on }A=\text{subsets of }A\times A:\ 2^{|A|^2}\)
Step 1: \(-1,2,0,3\in A\text{ and }|A|=4\Rightarrow A=\{-1,0,2,3\}\)
Step 2: \(\text{number of relations}=2^{16}\)
Step 3: \(y=x+3:\ x=-1\Rightarrow y=2\in A;\ x=0\Rightarrow y=3\in A;\ x=2,3\Rightarrow y=5,6\notin A\)
Worked derivation: \[R=\{(-1,2),(0,3)\};\ \text{domain}=\{-1,0\},\ \text{range}=\{2,3\}\]
Check: \[\text{A}\times\text{A as points: a }4\times4\text{ grid; R is the two grid points on the line }y=x+3\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{every coordinate of an ordered pair in }A\times A\text{ belongs to A; the four distinct numbers found already fill A}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(|A|=2\text{ gives only 4 pairs}\); (C) \(\text{16 is the number of pairs, not relations, and domain and range are swapped}\); (D) \(-1\text{ must be in A}\).
Key point: \(|A\times A|=|A|^2;\ \text{relations on A}=2^{|A|^2}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Domain and range of √(9 − x²) as a semicircle, and of x²/(1 + x²) as a bounded function
questions.question: What are the domain and range of \(f(x)=\sqrt{9-x^2}\) and the range of \(g(x)=\dfrac{x^2}{1+x^2}\) (with domain \(\mathbb R\))?
options: A) \(f:\ \text{domain }[-3,3],\ \text{range }[0,3];\ g:\ \text{range }[0,1)\)
B) \(f:\ \text{domain }\mathbb R,\ \text{range }[0,3];\ g:\ \text{range }[0,1]\)
C) \(f:\ \text{domain }[-3,3],\ \text{range }[-3,3];\ g:\ \text{range }(0,1)\)
D) \(f:\ \text{domain }[0,3],\ \text{range }[0,9];\ g:\ \text{range }[1,\infty)\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(f\): domain \([-3,3]\), range \([0,3]\); \(g\): range \([0,1)\).
Given: \(f(x)=\sqrt{9-x^2},\ g(x)=\dfrac{x^2}{1+x^2}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\sqrt{u}\text{ is real iff }u\ge0;\ \text{range from solving }y=g(x)\text{ for }x\)
Step 1: \(9-x^2\ge0\Rightarrow-3\le x\le3;\ 0\le9-x^2\le9\Rightarrow0\le f\le3\)
Step 2: \(y=\dfrac{x^2}{1+x^2}\Rightarrow x^2=\dfrac{y}{1-y}\ge0\Rightarrow0\le y<1\)
Worked derivation: \[y=\sqrt{9-x^2}\iff x^2+y^2=9,\ y\ge0\ (\text{upper semicircle});\qquad g(x)=1-\frac{1}{1+x^2}\in[0,1)\]
Check: \[g(0)=0;\ g(10)=\tfrac{100}{101}<1;\ g\text{ never equals 1}\ \checkmark;\ f(\pm3)=0,\ f(0)=3\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the graph of f is a semicircle of radius 3 above the x-axis; g approaches 1 as }|x|\to\infty\text{ but never reaches it}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(f\text{ is not real for }|x|>3;\ g\text{ never reaches 1}\); (C) \(\text{a square root is never negative, and }g(0)=0\); (D) \(\text{wrong domain and range for f, and }g\le1\).
Key point: \(\sqrt{9-x^2}:\ \text{upper semicircle};\ x^2/(1+x^2)\in[0,1)\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Converting radians to degrees, arc length on a circle, and the sign of sin at a large angle reduced by its period
questions.question: What is \(\dfrac{5\pi}{12}\) radian in degrees, what is the length of the arc that this angle cuts off on a circle of radius 12 cm, and what is \(\sin\dfrac{25\pi}{3}\)?
options: A) \(150^\circ;\ 10\pi\text{ cm};\ -\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\)
B) \(75^\circ;\ \tfrac{5\pi}{144}\text{ cm};\ \tfrac12\)
C) \(75^\circ;\ 5\pi\text{ cm}\approx15.7\text{ cm};\ \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\)
D) \(37.5^\circ;\ 5\pi\text{ cm};\ -\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(75^\circ\); \(5\pi\) cm; \(\tfrac{\sqrt3}2\).
Given: \(\theta=\tfrac{5\pi}{12},\ r=12\ \text{cm};\ \tfrac{25\pi}3\)
Formula/Principle: \(\pi\text{ rad}=180^\circ;\ l=r\theta;\ \sin(2n\pi+x)=\sin x\)
Step 1: \(\tfrac{5\pi}{12}\times\tfrac{180^\circ}{\pi}=75^\circ\)
Step 2: \(l=12\times\tfrac{5\pi}{12}=5\pi\approx15.7\ \text{cm}\)
Step 3: \(\tfrac{25\pi}{3}=8\pi+\tfrac\pi3\Rightarrow\sin\tfrac{25\pi}3=\sin\tfrac\pi3=\tfrac{\sqrt3}2\)
Worked derivation: \[l=r\theta\ (\theta\text{ in radians}):\ \frac{l}{2\pi r}=\frac{75^\circ}{360^\circ}\Rightarrow l=\frac{75}{360}\cdot24\pi=5\pi\]
Check: \[\tfrac{25\pi}{3}\text{ lies in the first quadrant after removing 4 full turns, where sine is positive}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{sine has period }2\pi\text{, so subtracting whole turns does not change its value; the arc formula needs the angle in radians}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{doubles the angle and gives the wrong quadrant}\); (B) \(\text{uses degrees in }l=r\theta\text{ wrongly, and }\sin\tfrac\pi3\ne\tfrac12\); (D) \(\text{halves the conversion and gets the sign wrong}\).
Key point: \(1\text{ rad}=180^\circ/\pi;\ l=r\theta;\ \text{reduce angles by }2\pi\text{ for sin and cos}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Showing (z − 1)/(z + 1) is purely imaginary when |z| = 1, with z = (1 + i)/(1 − i) as a special case
questions.question: Let \(z=\dfrac{1+i}{1-i}\). What are \(z\), \(z^{100}\) and \(\dfrac{z-1}{z+1}\)? Which general fact does this illustrate?
options: A) \(z=i,\ z^{100}=1,\ \dfrac{z-1}{z+1}=i\); if \(|z|=1\) and \(z\ne-1\), then \(\dfrac{z-1}{z+1}\) is purely imaginary (or zero)
D) \(z=i,\ z^{100}=i,\ \dfrac{z-1}{z+1}=-1\); the result holds only for real \(z\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(z=i\), \(z^{100}=1\), \(\dfrac{z-1}{z+1}=i\); for \(|z|=1\), \(\dfrac{z-1}{z+1}\) is purely imaginary.
Given: \(z=\dfrac{1+i}{1-i}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{multiply by the conjugate of the denominator};\ i^4=1;\ |z|=1\Rightarrow\bar z=\dfrac1z\)
Step 1: \(z=\dfrac{(1+i)^2}{(1-i)(1+i)}=\dfrac{2i}{2}=i\)
Step 2: \(z^{100}=i^{100}=(i^4)^{25}=1\)
Step 3: \(\dfrac{i-1}{i+1}=\dfrac{(i-1)(1-i)}{(1+i)(1-i)}=\dfrac{-1+2i+1}{2}=i\)
Worked derivation: \[w=\frac{z-1}{z+1}\Rightarrow\bar w=\frac{\bar z-1}{\bar z+1}=\frac{\frac1z-1}{\frac1z+1}=\frac{1-z}{1+z}=-w\Rightarrow w\text{ is purely imaginary (or 0)}\]
Check: \[z=\cos\theta+i\sin\theta:\ \frac{z-1}{z+1}=i\tan\frac\theta2;\ \theta=\tfrac\pi2:\ i\tan\tfrac\pi4=i\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{on the unit circle the conjugate equals the reciprocal, which makes }\bar w=-w\text{; geometrically, the angle subtended at z by the diameter from }-1\text{ to }1\text{ is a right angle}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(z\ne1\text{, and the quotient is imaginary, not real, for }|z|=1\); (C) \(\text{sign slip in }z\text{, and }|z|=1\text{ allows non-real z}\); (D) \(i^{100}=1\text{, and }\tfrac{i-1}{i+1}=i\).
Key point: \(|z|=1,\ z\ne-1\Rightarrow\dfrac{z-1}{z+1}\in i\mathbb R\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Counting parallelograms formed by two families of parallel lines, and diagonals of a decagon, by choosing pairs
questions.question: A set of 4 parallel lines is cut by another set of 5 parallel lines (not parallel to the first set). How many parallelograms are formed? Also, how many diagonals does a convex decagon have?
options: A) 20 parallelograms; 45 diagonals
B) 9 parallelograms; 35 diagonals
C) 60 parallelograms; 45 diagonals
D) 60 parallelograms; 35 diagonals
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 60 parallelograms; 35 diagonals.
Given: \(4\text{ lines in one family, 5 in the other};\ \text{decagon: 10 vertices}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{a parallelogram needs 2 lines from each family};\ \text{diagonals}=\binom n2-n\)
Step 1: \(\binom42\times\binom52=6\times10=60\)
Step 2: \(\binom{10}{2}-10=45-10=35\)
Worked derivation: \[\text{each choice of two lines from each family bounds exactly one parallelogram};\ \text{a segment joining two vertices is a side or a diagonal}\]
Check: \[\text{diagonals}=\frac{n(n-3)}{2}=\frac{10\cdot7}{2}=35\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the geometric figure is fixed by the lines chosen, so counting figures reduces to counting selections; sides are not diagonals, so the n sides are removed}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{multiplies the line counts, and 45 includes the sides}\); (B) \(\text{adds the line counts}\); (C) \(\text{45 counts the 10 sides as diagonals}\).
Key point: \(\text{parallelograms}=\binom m2\binom n2;\ \text{diagonals}=n(n-3)/2\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Areas of squares formed by repeatedly joining the midpoints of the sides as a geometric progression
questions.question: A square has side 10 cm. A second square is formed by joining the midpoints of its sides, a third by joining the midpoints of the second, and so on. What is the sum of the areas of the first six squares, and what is the side of the seventh square?
options: A) \(600\ \text{cm}^2;\ \tfrac{10}{\sqrt2}\ \text{cm}\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(196.875\ \text{cm}^2\); side \(1.25\) cm.
Given: \(\text{side}_1=10;\ \text{each new side}=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\times\text{previous side}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{G.P.: }a_n=ar^{n-1},\ S_n=\dfrac{a(1-r^n)}{1-r}\)
Step 1: \(\text{areas: }100,50,25,\ldots;\ a=100,\ r=\tfrac12\)
Step 2: \(S_6=\dfrac{100\left(1-\tfrac1{64}\right)}{\tfrac12}=200\cdot\dfrac{63}{64}=196.875\)
Step 3: \(\text{side}_7=10\left(\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\right)^6=\dfrac{10}{8}=1.25\ \text{cm}\)
Worked derivation: \[\text{new side}=\sqrt{\left(\tfrac s2\right)^2+\left(\tfrac s2\right)^2}=\frac{s}{\sqrt2}\Rightarrow\text{area ratio}=\tfrac12\]
Check: \[100+50+25+12.5+6.25+3.125=196.875\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{each inner square has its corners at the midpoints, so its side is the hypotenuse of a right triangle with legs }s/2\text{; areas therefore halve each time, forming a G.P.}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{adds six equal areas, and gives the second side, not the seventh}\); (B) \(200\text{ is the limit of the infinite sum, not }S_6\); (D) \(\text{uses ratio }\tfrac12\text{ for sides instead of }\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\).
Key point: \(\text{midpoint squares: sides ratio }1/\sqrt2,\ \text{areas ratio }1/2\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Finding the constant c of a line from its distance to a given point, and writing the line in normal form
questions.question: For which values of \(c\) is the distance of the point \((1,2)\) from the line \(3x-4y+c=0\) equal to 2? For the positive value, write the line in normal form \(x\cos\omega+y\sin\omega=p\) with \(p>0\).
options: B) \(c=15\text{ or }c=-5\); \(-\tfrac35x+\tfrac45y=3\), so \(p=3\)
D) \(c=15\text{ or }c=-5\); \(\tfrac35x-\tfrac45y=3\), so \(p=3\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(c=15\) or \(-5\); for \(c=15\): \(-\tfrac35x+\tfrac45y=3\), \(p=3\).
Given: \(\text{point }(1,2);\ \text{line }3x-4y+c=0;\ d=2\)
Formula/Principle: \(d=\dfrac{|Ax_1+By_1+C|}{\sqrt{A^2+B^2}};\ \text{normal form: divide by }\pm\sqrt{A^2+B^2}\text{ so the constant on the right is positive}\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{|3-8+c|}{5}=2\Rightarrow|c-5|=10\Rightarrow c=15\text{ or }-5\)
Step 2: \(c=15:\ 3x-4y+15=0\Rightarrow-3x+4y=15\Rightarrow-\tfrac35x+\tfrac45y=3\)
Worked derivation: \[\cos\omega=-\tfrac35,\ \sin\omega=\tfrac45\ (\omega\text{ in the second quadrant}),\ p=3=\text{distance of the line from the origin}\]
Check: \[\text{distance of }(0,0)\text{ from }3x-4y+15=0:\ \tfrac{15}{5}=3\ \checkmark;\ \text{from }(1,2):\ \tfrac{|3-8+15|}{5}=2\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the absolute value gives two parallel lines, one on each side of the point; in normal form, p is the perpendicular distance from the origin, so it must be positive}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{misses the second line, and p is wrong}\); (C) \(\text{forgets the }3-8\text{ term}\); (D) \(\tfrac35x-\tfrac45y=3\text{ means }3x-4y-15=0\text{, a different line}\).
Key point: \(|Ax_1+By_1+C|=d\sqrt{A^2+B^2}\text{ gives two lines; normal form has }p>0\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Counting integer values of k for which x² + y² − 4x + 6y + k = 0 is a real circle, a point circle or no real locus
questions.question: For how many integers \(k\) with \(0\le k\le20\) does \(x^2+y^2-4x+6y+k=0\) represent a real circle of positive radius, and for how many does it reduce to a single point (a degenerate case, like a plane through the vertex of a cone cutting it in a single point)?
options: A) 12 real circles; 2 point circles
B) 14 real circles; 0 point circles
C) 13 real circles; 1 point circle
D) 20 real circles; 1 point circle
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 13 circles; 1 point circle (at \(k=13\)).
Given: \(x^2+y^2-4x+6y+k=0\)
Formula/Principle: \((x-2)^2+(y+3)^2=13-k;\ r^2=g^2+f^2-c\)
Step 1: \(\text{real circle}\iff13-k>0\iff k<13\Rightarrow k=0,1,\ldots,12\ (13\text{ values})\)
Step 2: \(k=13\Rightarrow(x-2)^2+(y+3)^2=0\Rightarrow\text{only the point }(2,-3)\)
Step 3: \(k=14,\ldots,20\Rightarrow r^2<0\Rightarrow\text{no real points (7 values)}\)
Worked derivation: \[13+1+7=21=\text{number of integers from 0 to 20}\]
Check: \[k=12:\ r=1;\ k=13:\ r=0;\ k=14:\ (x-2)^2+(y+3)^2=-1\ \text{(impossible)}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{completing the square shows the radius directly; when it shrinks to zero the circle degenerates to its centre, just as a conic degenerates when the cutting plane passes through the vertex of the cone}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{misses one circle, and there is only one point circle}\); (B) \(\text{counts }k=13\text{ as a circle}\); (D) \(\text{ignores the condition }k<13\).
Key point: \(r^2=g^2+f^2-c:\ >0\text{ circle},\ =0\text{ point},\ <0\text{ none}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: The circle touching the x-axis at (4, 0) and passing through (1, 9), and a second circle touching it externally at the same point
questions.question: A circle touches the \(x\)-axis at \((4,0)\) and passes through \((1,9)\). What is its equation? A second circle of radius 3 touches the first externally at \((4,0)\). What is the equation of the second circle?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \((x-4)^2+(y-5)^2=25\); \(x^2+y^2-8x+6y+16=0\).
Given: \(\text{touches the x-axis at }(4,0);\ \text{passes through }(1,9);\ \text{second radius }3\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{touching the x-axis at }(a,0)\Rightarrow\text{centre }(a,k),\ r=|k|;\ \text{external contact: distance between centres}=r_1+r_2\)
Step 1: \((1-4)^2+(9-k)^2=k^2\Rightarrow9+81-18k=0\Rightarrow k=5\)
Step 2: \(\text{first circle: centre }(4,5),\ r=5\)
Step 3: \(\text{second centre on the common normal }x=4\text{ below the axis: }(4,-3)\Rightarrow(x-4)^2+(y+3)^2=9\)
Worked derivation: \[(x-4)^2+(y+3)^2=9\iff x^2+y^2-8x+6y+16=0;\qquad\text{distance between centres}=5-(-3)=8=5+3\]
Check: \[(1,9):\ 9+16=25\ \checkmark;\ (4,0)\text{ lies on both circles}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the radius to the point of contact is perpendicular to the tangent (the x-axis), so both centres lie on the line }x=4\text{, on opposite sides of the axis for external contact}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{puts the second centre at }(4,3)\text{, inside the first circle (internal contact)}\); (C) \(\text{takes the given point's y-coordinate as the radius}\); (D) \(\text{uses the given point as the centre}\).
Key point: \(\text{tangent to the x-axis at }(a,0):\ \text{centre }(a,r);\ \text{external contact: }d=r_1+r_2\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Finding n from the value of lim (xⁿ − aⁿ)/(x − a), interpreted as the derivative of xⁿ at a
questions.question: For a positive integer \(n\), \(\displaystyle\lim_{x\to2}\frac{x^n-2^n}{x-2}=80\). What is \(n\), and what does this limit represent?
options: A) \(n=4\); the area under \(y=x^n\) from 0 to 2
B) \(n=40\); the average value of \(x^n\)
C) \(n=6\); the second derivative of \(x^n\) at 2
D) \(n=5\); the derivative of \(x^n\) at \(x=2\), found from first principles, equal to \(n\cdot2^{n-1}\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(n=5\); the limit is \(f'(2)\) for \(f(x)=x^n\).
Given: \(\displaystyle\lim_{x\to2}\frac{x^n-2^n}{x-2}=80\)
Formula/Principle: \(\displaystyle\lim_{x\to a}\frac{x^n-a^n}{x-a}=na^{n-1};\ f'(a)=\lim_{x\to a}\frac{f(x)-f(a)}{x-a}\)
Step 1: \(n\cdot2^{n-1}=80\)
Step 2: \(n=5:\ 5\cdot16=80\ \checkmark;\ n\cdot2^{n-1}\text{ increases with n, so this is the only solution}\)
Worked derivation: \[\frac{x^n-a^n}{x-a}=x^{n-1}+x^{n-2}a+\cdots+a^{n-1}\to na^{n-1}\ (x\to a)\]
Check: \[n=4:\ 4\cdot8=32;\ n=6:\ 6\cdot32=192;\ \text{only }n=5\text{ gives }80\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the expression is the slope of the chord from }(2,2^n)\text{ to }(x,x^n)\text{; as }x\to2\text{ it becomes the slope of the tangent, which is the derivative and the instantaneous rate of change}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(4\cdot2^3=32\ne80\text{, and the limit is a slope, not an area}\); (B) \(\text{ignores the }2^{n-1}\text{ factor}\); (C) \(6\cdot2^5=192\ne80\text{, and this is a first derivative}\).
Key point: \(\lim_{x\to a}(x^n-a^n)/(x-a)=na^{n-1}=\tfrac{d}{dx}x^n\big|_{a}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Range of a parameter that makes a probability assignment valid on a four-outcome sample space, and its value under an extra condition
questions.question: A sample space is \(S=\{a,b,c,d\}\), with \(P(a)=p,\ P(b)=2p,\ P(c)=p^2\) and \(P(d)=1-3p-p^2\). For which \(p\) is this a valid assignment of probabilities? If also \(P(d)=P(a)\), what is \(p\), and what is \(P(\{a,b\})\)?
options: A) \(0\le p\le\tfrac13\); \(p=\tfrac14\); \(P=\tfrac34\)
B) \(0\le p\le\dfrac{\sqrt{13}-3}{2}\approx0.303\); \(p=\sqrt5-2\approx0.236\); \(P(\{a,b\})=3\sqrt5-6\approx0.708\)
D) \(p\ge0\) only; \(p=\tfrac12\); \(P=\tfrac32\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(0\le p\le\tfrac{\sqrt{13}-3}{2}\); \(p=\sqrt5-2\); \(P(\{a,b\})=3\sqrt5-6\).
Given: \(P(a)=p,\ P(b)=2p,\ P(c)=p^2,\ P(d)=1-3p-p^2\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{each }P(\omega)\ge0\text{ and the probabilities sum to 1 (here the sum is 1 automatically)}\)
Step 1: \(p\ge0\text{ (makes }P(a),P(b),P(c)\ge0)\)
Step 2: \(1-3p-p^2\ge0\iff p^2+3p-1\le0\iff p\le\dfrac{-3+\sqrt{13}}{2}\approx0.303\)
Step 3: \(1-3p-p^2=p\Rightarrow p^2+4p-1=0\Rightarrow p=-2+\sqrt5\approx0.236\ (\text{positive root, within range})\)
Worked derivation: \[P(\{a,b\})=3p=3(\sqrt5-2)=3\sqrt5-6\approx0.708\]
Check: \[p=0.236:\ P=0.236,\ 0.472,\ 0.0557,\ 0.236;\ \text{sum}=1.000\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{a valid assignment needs every outcome to have a non-negative probability; the binding condition is on }P(d)\text{, the leftover probability}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(p=\tfrac14\text{ gives }P(d)=1-\tfrac34-\tfrac1{16}=\tfrac3{16}\ne\tfrac14\); (C) \(p=1\text{ gives }P(d)=-3\), \(\text{and }P(\{a,b\})=3p\); (D) \(\text{a probability cannot exceed 1}\).
Key point: \(\text{valid assignment: all }P(\omega)\ge0,\ \sum P(\omega)=1\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Number of solutions of cos⁻¹x = 2 sin⁻¹x, and counting integers in the domain of sin⁻¹((x − 1)/2) + cos⁻¹(x/3)
questions.question: How many real \(x\) satisfy \(\cos^{-1}x=2\sin^{-1}x\)? How many integers lie in the domain of \(f(x)=\sin^{-1}\dfrac{x-1}{2}+\cos^{-1}\dfrac x3\)?
options: A) 2 solutions; 7 integers
B) No solution; 4 integers
C) 1 solution; 7 integers
D) 1 solution \(\left(x=\tfrac12\right)\); 5 integers
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) One solution, \(x=\tfrac12\); 5 integers.
Given: \(\cos^{-1}x=2\sin^{-1}x;\ f(x)=\sin^{-1}\frac{x-1}{2}+\cos^{-1}\frac x3\)
Formula/Principle: \(\sin^{-1}x+\cos^{-1}x=\dfrac\pi2,\ |x|\le1;\ \text{domain of }\sin^{-1}u,\cos^{-1}u:\ -1\le u\le1\)
Step 1: \(\tfrac\pi2-\sin^{-1}x=2\sin^{-1}x\Rightarrow\sin^{-1}x=\tfrac\pi6\Rightarrow x=\tfrac12\ (\text{unique, as }\sin^{-1}\text{ is one-one})\)
Step 2: \(-1\le\tfrac{x-1}{2}\le1\Rightarrow-1\le x\le3;\ -1\le\tfrac x3\le1\Rightarrow-3\le x\le3\)
Step 3: \(\text{domain}=[-1,3]\Rightarrow\text{integers }-1,0,1,2,3\ (5)\)
Worked derivation: \[x=\tfrac12:\ \cos^{-1}\tfrac12=\tfrac\pi3,\ 2\sin^{-1}\tfrac12=2\cdot\tfrac\pi6=\tfrac\pi3\ \checkmark\]
Check: \[x=4:\ \tfrac{x-1}{2}=1.5>1\Rightarrow\text{outside the domain}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the identity turns the equation into one with a single inverse function, which takes each value once; the domain of a sum is the intersection of the domains of its terms}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{the principal-value function is one-one, so there is only one root; the domain is the intersection, not the union}\); (B) \(x=\tfrac12\text{ works, and the count misses an endpoint}\); (C) \(\text{the domain is }[-1,3]\text{, not }[-3,3]\).
Key point: \(\sin^{-1}x+\cos^{-1}x=\tfrac\pi2;\ \text{domain of a sum = intersection of domains}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Conditions on λ and μ for a 3 × 3 system to have a unique solution, infinitely many solutions or none, with the general solution in the dependent case
questions.question: For the system \(x+y+2z=4,\ 2x-y+z=3,\ x-2y+\lambda z=\mu\), which statement is correct?
options: A) Unique solution for every \(\lambda\)
B) Unique solution iff \(\lambda\ne1\); infinitely many iff \(\lambda=1,\ \mu=1\)

C) Unique solution iff \(\lambda\ne-1\); infinitely many solutions, \((x,y,z)=\left(\tfrac73-t,\tfrac53-t,t\right)\), iff \(\lambda=-1\) and \(\mu=-1\); no solution iff \(\lambda=-1\) and \(\mu\ne-1\)
D) Unique solution iff \(\lambda=-1\); no solution iff \(\mu=-1\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Unique iff \(\lambda\ne-1\); infinite iff \(\lambda=-1,\ \mu=-1\); none iff \(\lambda=-1,\ \mu\ne-1\).
Given: \(A=\begin{pmatrix}1&1&2\\2&-1&1\\1&-2&\lambda\end{pmatrix},\ B=\begin{pmatrix}4\\3\\\mu\end{pmatrix}\)
Formula/Principle: \(|A|\ne0\Rightarrow\text{unique solution};\ |A|=0\Rightarrow\text{infinitely many or none, depending on consistency}\)
Step 1: \(|A|=1(-\lambda+2)-1(2\lambda-1)+2(-4+1)=-3\lambda-3\Rightarrow|A|=0\iff\lambda=-1\)
Step 2: \(\lambda=-1:\ \text{row}_3=\text{row}_2-\text{row}_1\text{ on the left}\Rightarrow\text{consistent iff }\mu=3-4=-1\)
Step 3: \(z=t:\ x+y=4-2t,\ 2x-y=3-t\Rightarrow x=\tfrac73-t,\ y=\tfrac53-t\)
Worked derivation: \[\text{eq}_3:\ \left(\tfrac73-t\right)-2\left(\tfrac53-t\right)-t=\tfrac73-\tfrac{10}3=-1=\mu\ \checkmark\]
Check: \[t=0:\ \left(\tfrac73,\tfrac53,0\right):\ \tfrac73+\tfrac53=4\ \checkmark;\ \tfrac{14}3-\tfrac53=3\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{when the determinant vanishes, the third equation's left side is a combination of the first two; it must then match on the right side as well, or the equations contradict each other}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(|A|=0\text{ at }\lambda=-1\); (B) \(\text{sign error in the determinant}\); (D) \(\text{reverses the condition for a unique solution}\).
Key point: \(|A|\ne0\text{: unique};\ |A|=0\text{: check whether the right-hand sides satisfy the same dependence}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Derivative of cos⁻¹((1 − x²)/(1 + x²)) on x > 0 and x < 0, the corner at x = 0, and an implicit derivative on a circle
questions.question: For \(y=\cos^{-1}\dfrac{1-x^2}{1+x^2}\), what is \(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\) for \(x>0\) and for \(x<0\), and is \(y\) differentiable at \(x=0\)? Also, what is the slope of \(x^2+y^2=25\) at \((3,4)\)?
options: A) \(\dfrac{2}{1+x^2}\) for all \(x\), differentiable at 0; \(\tfrac34\)
B) \(\dfrac{2}{1+x^2}\) for \(x>0\), \(-\dfrac{2}{1+x^2}\) for \(x<0\); not differentiable at 0 (left and right derivatives \(-2\) and \(2\)); \(-\tfrac34\)
C) \(\dfrac{1}{1+x^2}\) for \(x>0\); differentiable at 0; \(-\tfrac43\)
D) \(-\dfrac{2}{1+x^2}\) for \(x>0\); differentiable at 0; \(-\tfrac34\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(\tfrac{2}{1+x^2}\) for \(x>0\), \(-\tfrac{2}{1+x^2}\) for \(x<0\); not differentiable at 0; slope \(-\tfrac34\).
Given: \(y=\cos^{-1}\dfrac{1-x^2}{1+x^2};\ x^2+y^2=25\)
Formula/Principle: \(x=\tan\theta\Rightarrow\dfrac{1-x^2}{1+x^2}=\cos2\theta;\ \cos^{-1}(\cos u)=u\text{ only for }u\in[0,\pi]\)
Step 1: \(x\ge0\Rightarrow\theta\in\left[0,\tfrac\pi2\right)\Rightarrow2\theta\in[0,\pi)\Rightarrow y=2\tan^{-1}x\Rightarrow y'=\dfrac{2}{1+x^2}\)
Step 2: \(x<0\Rightarrow2\theta\in(-\pi,0)\Rightarrow y=-2\theta=-2\tan^{-1}x\Rightarrow y'=-\dfrac{2}{1+x^2}\)
Step 3: \(\text{at }x=0:\ \text{right derivative }2,\ \text{left derivative }-2\Rightarrow\text{not differentiable};\ \text{circle: }y'=-\dfrac xy=-\dfrac34\)
Worked derivation: \[y=2\left|\tan^{-1}x\right|\ \text{for all real }x;\ \text{like }|x|\text{, it has a corner at }x=0\]
Check: \[x=1:\ y=\cos^{-1}0=\tfrac\pi2=2\tan^{-1}1\ \checkmark;\ x=-1:\ y=\tfrac\pi2=-2\tan^{-1}(-1)\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\cos^{-1}\text{ returns values only in }[0,\pi]\text{, so for negative x the simple substitution must be corrected by a sign, which produces a corner at the origin}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{ignores the change of formula for }x<0\text{, and the circle's slope is negative there}\); (C) \(\text{drops the factor 2 and inverts the slope}\); (D) \(\text{wrong sign for }x>0\).
Key point: \(\cos^{-1}\frac{1-x^2}{1+x^2}=2|\tan^{-1}x|;\ \text{check principal ranges before substituting}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Finding the edge of a growing cube from the rates of change of its volume and edge, then the rate of change of its surface area
questions.question: The edge of a cube is increasing at 0.2 cm/s. At a certain instant, its volume is increasing at 15 cm³/s. What is the edge at that instant, and how fast is the surface area increasing then?
options: A) 5 cm; 12 cm²/s
B) 25 cm; 60 cm²/s
C) 5 cm; 6 cm²/s
D) \(\sqrt{75}\) cm; 12 cm²/s
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Edge 5 cm; surface area increasing at 12 cm²/s.
Given: \(\dfrac{dx}{dt}=0.2\ \text{cm/s},\ \dfrac{dV}{dt}=15\ \text{cm}^3/\text{s}\)
Formula/Principle: \(V=x^3\Rightarrow\dfrac{dV}{dt}=3x^2\dfrac{dx}{dt};\ S=6x^2\Rightarrow\dfrac{dS}{dt}=12x\dfrac{dx}{dt}\)
Step 1: \(15=3x^2(0.2)=0.6x^2\Rightarrow x^2=25\Rightarrow x=5\ \text{cm}\)
Step 2: \(\dfrac{dS}{dt}=12(5)(0.2)=12\ \text{cm}^2/\text{s}\)
Worked derivation: \[\frac{dS/dt}{dV/dt}=\frac{12x}{3x^2}=\frac4x\Rightarrow\frac{dS}{dt}=\frac45\times15=12\]
Check: \[3(25)(0.2)=15\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{both rates come from the chain rule through the same edge rate; the given volume rate fixes the edge, which then fixes every other rate}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{takes }x^2\text{ as the edge}\); (C) \(\text{uses }dS/dt=6x\,dx/dt\text{, forgetting to differentiate }x^2\); (D) \(\text{solves }15=0.2x^2\text{, dropping the factor 3}\).
Key point: \(\text{chain rule: }dV/dt=3x^2\,dx/dt,\ dS/dt=12x\,dx/dt\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Finding the positive upper limit a for which ∫₀ᵃ x eˣ dx = 1, and the e^x(f + f′) form
questions.question: For which positive \(a\) is \(\displaystyle\int_0^{a}xe^{x}\,dx=1\)? Also, what is \(\displaystyle\int e^{x}(\tan x+\sec^2x)\,dx\)?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(a=1\); \(e^{x}\tan x+C\).
Given: \(\displaystyle\int_0^axe^x\,dx=1,\ a>0\)
Formula/Principle: \(\displaystyle\int u\,v\,dx=u\int v\,dx-\int\left(u'\int v\,dx\right)dx;\ \int e^x\big(f(x)+f'(x)\big)dx=e^xf(x)+C\)
Step 1: \(\displaystyle\int xe^x\,dx=xe^x-e^x=e^x(x-1)\)
Step 2: \([e^x(x-1)]_0^a=e^a(a-1)-(-1)=e^a(a-1)+1=1\Rightarrow e^a(a-1)=0\Rightarrow a=1\)
Step 3: \(f(x)=\tan x,\ f'(x)=\sec^2x\Rightarrow\displaystyle\int e^x(\tan x+\sec^2x)dx=e^x\tan x+C\)
Worked derivation: \[\frac{d}{dx}\big(e^x\tan x\big)=e^x\tan x+e^x\sec^2x\ \checkmark;\qquad\frac{d}{dx}\big(e^x(x-1)\big)=e^x(x-1)+e^x=xe^x\ \checkmark\]
Check: \[\int_0^1xe^x\,dx=e(0)+1=1\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{taking }u=x\text{ removes the polynomial factor after one differentiation; since }e^a>0\text{, the condition forces }a-1=0\)
Why not the others: (A) \(e^{\ln2}(\ln2-1)\ne0\), \(\text{and }\tfrac{d}{dx}(e^x\sec^2x)\ne e^x(\tan x+\sec^2x)\); (C) \(e^2(1)+1=e^2+1\ne1\); (D) \(a=e\text{ does not satisfy }a-1=0\text{, and the antiderivative is wrong}\).
Key point: \(\int xe^x\,dx=e^x(x-1);\ \int e^x(f+f')\,dx=e^xf\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Classifying ∫ dx/(x² + 6x + k) as a tan⁻¹, rational or logarithmic form for integer k, and a square-root standard form
questions.question: For integers \(k\) with \(0\le k\le15\), the integral \(\displaystyle\int\frac{dx}{x^2+6x+k}\) takes one of three forms. For how many \(k\) is it a \(\tan^{-1}\) form, for how many a purely rational function, and for how many a logarithmic form? Also, what is \(\displaystyle\int\frac{dx}{\sqrt{x^2+6x+13}}\)?
options: C) 6, 1, 9; \(\log\left|x+3+\sqrt{x^2+6x+13}\right|+C\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 6 \(\tan^{-1}\) forms, 1 rational, 9 logarithmic; \(\log\left|x+3+\sqrt{x^2+6x+13}\right|+C\).
Given: \(x^2+6x+k=(x+3)^2+(k-9)\)
Formula/Principle: \(\displaystyle\int\frac{dx}{u^2+a^2}=\frac1a\tan^{-1}\frac ua;\ \int\frac{dx}{u^2}=-\frac1u;\ \int\frac{dx}{u^2-a^2}=\frac1{2a}\log\left|\frac{u-a}{u+a}\right|;\ \int\frac{dx}{\sqrt{u^2+a^2}}=\log\left|u+\sqrt{u^2+a^2}\right|\)
Step 1: \(k>9:\ k=10,\ldots,15\Rightarrow6\text{ values }(\tan^{-1})\)
Step 2: \(k=9:\ \displaystyle\int\frac{dx}{(x+3)^2}=-\frac1{x+3}+C\ (\text{rational})\)
Step 3: \(k<9:\ k=0,\ldots,8\Rightarrow9\text{ values }(\text{log form})\)
Worked derivation: \[x^2+6x+13=(x+3)^2+2^2\Rightarrow\int\frac{dx}{\sqrt{(x+3)^2+4}}=\log\left|x+3+\sqrt{x^2+6x+13}\right|+C\]
Check: \[6+1+9=16=\text{number of integers from 0 to 15}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{completing the square shows whether the quadratic is a sum of squares (no real roots), a perfect square or a difference of squares (two real roots); that decides the standard form}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{counts }k=9\text{ as a }\tan^{-1}\text{ form; the square-root form here is a log, not }\sin^{-1}\); (B) \(\text{miscounts the boundary, and the antiderivative is wrong}\); (D) \(k=9\text{ gives a rational result, and the square-root integral is not a }\tan^{-1}\).
Key point: \(\text{complete the square: }+a^2\to\tan^{-1},\ 0\to\text{rational},\ -a^2\to\log\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Values of m for which y = e^{mx} solves y″ − 5y′ + 6y = 0, with the order and degree of a differential equation
questions.question: For which values of \(m\) is \(y=e^{mx}\) a solution of \(y''-5y'+6y=0\)? What are the order and degree of \((y'')^3+(y')^4+y=0\), and what is the order of the differential equation whose general solution is \(y=Ae^{2x}+Be^{3x}\)?
options: A) \(m=-2,-3\); order 3, degree 2; order 1
B) \(m=1,6\); order 2, degree 4; order 2
C) \(m=2\text{ only}\); order 2, degree 3; order 3
D) \(m=2\text{ or }3\); order 2, degree 3; order 2
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(m=2\) or \(3\); order 2, degree 3; order 2.
Given: \(y=e^{mx}\Rightarrow y'=me^{mx},\ y''=m^2e^{mx}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{order = highest derivative; degree = power of that derivative (polynomial in derivatives)};\ \text{number of arbitrary constants = order}\)
Step 1: \(e^{mx}(m^2-5m+6)=0\Rightarrow(m-2)(m-3)=0\Rightarrow m=2,3\)
Step 2: \((y'')^3+(y')^4+y=0:\ \text{highest derivative }y''\Rightarrow\text{order 2; its power 3}\Rightarrow\text{degree 3}\)
Step 3: \(y=Ae^{2x}+Be^{3x}\text{ has 2 arbitrary constants}\Rightarrow\text{order 2 (it is }y''-5y'+6y=0)\)
Worked derivation: \[y=Ae^{2x}+Be^{3x}:\ y'=2Ae^{2x}+3Be^{3x},\ y''=4Ae^{2x}+9Be^{3x};\ y''-5y'+6y=(4-10+6)Ae^{2x}+(9-15+6)Be^{3x}=0\]
Check: \[m=3:\ 9-15+6=0\ \checkmark;\ m=2:\ 4-10+6=0\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(e^{mx}\text{ is never zero, so the equation reduces to a quadratic in m; eliminating two constants needs two differentiations, giving a second-order equation}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{sign slip, and the order is fixed by }y''\); (B) \(\text{wrong roots, and degree is the power of the highest-order derivative}\); (C) \(\text{misses }m=3\text{, and two constants give order 2}\).
Key point: \(e^{mx}\text{ trial gives the auxiliary quadratic; order = number of arbitrary constants}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Area of a parallelogram from its diagonal vectors using the cross product, and a unit vector perpendicular to its plane
questions.question: A parallelogram has diagonals \(\vec d_1=3\hat i+\hat j-2\hat k\) and \(\vec d_2=\hat i-3\hat j+4\hat k\). What is its area, and which is a unit vector perpendicular to its plane?
options: A) \(5\sqrt3;\ \dfrac{1}{5\sqrt3}(\hat i+7\hat j+5\hat k)\)
B) \(10\sqrt3;\ \dfrac{1}{5\sqrt3}(\hat i-7\hat j+5\hat k)\)
C) \(\tfrac52\sqrt3;\ \hat i+7\hat j+5\hat k\)
D) \(5\sqrt3;\ \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{14}}(3\hat i+\hat j-2\hat k)\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Area \(5\sqrt3\); unit normal \(\tfrac{1}{5\sqrt3}(\hat i+7\hat j+5\hat k)\).
Given: \(\vec d_1=(3,1,-2),\ \vec d_2=(1,-3,4)\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{sides }\vec a,\vec b\Rightarrow\vec d_1=\vec a+\vec b,\ \vec d_2=\vec a-\vec b;\ \vec d_1\times\vec d_2=-2(\vec a\times\vec b)\Rightarrow\text{area}=\tfrac12|\vec d_1\times\vec d_2|\)
Step 1: \(\vec d_1\times\vec d_2=\big(1\cdot4-(-2)(-3),\ (-2)(1)-3\cdot4,\ 3(-3)-1\cdot1\big)=(-2,-14,-10)\)
Step 2: \(|\vec d_1\times\vec d_2|=\sqrt{4+196+100}=\sqrt{300}=10\sqrt3\Rightarrow\text{area}=5\sqrt3\)
Step 3: \(\hat n=\pm\dfrac{(-2,-14,-10)}{10\sqrt3}=\pm\dfrac{(1,7,5)}{5\sqrt3}\)
Worked derivation: \[(\vec a+\vec b)\times(\vec a-\vec b)=\vec a\times\vec a-\vec a\times\vec b+\vec b\times\vec a-\vec b\times\vec b=-2\,\vec a\times\vec b\]
Check: \[(1,7,5)\cdot(3,1,-2)=3+7-10=0;\ (1,7,5)\cdot(1,-3,4)=1-21+20=0\ \checkmark;\ |(1,7,5)|=\sqrt{75}=5\sqrt3\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the diagonals' cross product is twice the sides' cross product, whose magnitude is the area; its direction is perpendicular to both diagonals, hence to the plane}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{forgets the factor }\tfrac12\text{, and }(1,-7,5)\text{ is not perpendicular to }\vec d_1\); (C) \(\text{halves twice, and the vector is not a unit vector}\); (D) \(\text{this unit vector lies along a diagonal, in the plane}\).
Key point: \(\text{parallelogram area}=\tfrac12|\vec d_1\times\vec d_2|=|\vec a\times\vec b|\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: What Kepler's laws say about a planet's speed and period, and why the areal velocity is constant
questions.question: A planet moves in an elliptical orbit with the Sun at one focus. Its distance from the Sun is \(r_p\) at perihelion and \(r_a\) at aphelion. Which statement is correct?
options: A) The planet moves fastest at aphelion, because it has travelled farthest from the Sun

B) The line joining the Sun and the planet sweeps out equal areas in equal times, because the gravitational force is central and exerts no torque about the Sun, so the planet's angular momentum is conserved; hence \(v_p/v_a=r_a/r_p\), the planet is fastest at perihelion, and the square of its period is proportional to the cube of the semi-major axis
C) The areal velocity is constant only for circular orbits
D) The period depends on the mass of the planet, so heavier planets at the same distance take longer
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Constant areal velocity (angular momentum conservation); \(v_p/v_a=r_a/r_p\); \(T^2\propto a^3\).
Given: \(\text{perihelion distance }r_p,\ \text{aphelion distance }r_a\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{Kepler's second law: }\dfrac{\Delta A}{\Delta t}=\dfrac{L}{2m}=\text{constant};\ \text{third law: }T^2\propto a^3\)
Step 1: \(\text{at perihelion and aphelion, }\vec v\perp\vec r\Rightarrow L=mv_pr_p=mv_ar_a\)
Step 2: \(\dfrac{v_p}{v_a}=\dfrac{r_a}{r_p}>1\Rightarrow\text{fastest at perihelion}\)
Worked derivation: \[\Delta A=\tfrac12|\vec r\times\vec v\,\Delta t|\Rightarrow\frac{\Delta A}{\Delta t}=\frac{|\vec r\times\vec p|}{2m}=\frac{L}{2m};\qquad\vec\tau=\vec r\times\vec F=0\text{ (central force)}\Rightarrow L\text{ constant}\]
Check: \[\text{circular orbit: }T^2=\frac{4\pi^2}{GM}r^3\text{, independent of the planet's mass}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{gravity always points along the line to the Sun, so it cannot change the planet's angular momentum about the Sun; to keep L fixed, the planet must move faster when it is closer}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{the planet is slowest at aphelion}\); (C) \(\text{the second law holds for any orbit under a central force}\); (D) \(T^2=4\pi^2a^3/GM\text{ depends on the Sun's mass, not the planet's}\).
Key point: \(\text{equal areas in equal times}\iff L\text{ conserved};\ v\propto1/r\text{ at the apsides};\ T^2\propto a^3\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: How force and distance scale in a hydraulic lift, and how pressure scales with depth in water
questions.question: A hydraulic lift has pistons of areas \(A_1\) and \(A_2=100A_1\). A force of 50 N is applied to the small piston, which moves down 20 cm. What force acts on the large piston and how far does it rise? Also, compare the absolute pressure at depths of 10 m and 20 m in water (\(\rho=1000\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}\), \(g=9.8\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\), \(P_a=1.01\times10^{5}\) Pa).
options: A) 50 N; 20 cm; the pressure at 20 m is twice that at 10 m
B) 500 N; 2 cm; the pressure at 20 m equals that at 10 m
C) 5000 N; 0.2 cm; about \(1.99\times10^5\) Pa at 10 m and \(2.97\times10^5\) Pa at 20 m, so doubling the depth does not double the absolute pressure
D) 5000 N; 20 cm; the pressure at 20 m is four times that at 10 m
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 5000 N; rises 0.2 cm; about 1.99 × 10⁵ Pa and 2.97 × 10⁵ Pa.
Given: \(A_2/A_1=100,\ F_1=50\ \mathrm N,\ d_1=20\ \mathrm{cm}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{Pascal's law: }\dfrac{F_1}{A_1}=\dfrac{F_2}{A_2};\ \text{volume conserved: }A_1d_1=A_2d_2;\ P=P_a+\rho gh\)
Step 1: \(F_2=50\times100=5000\ \mathrm N;\ d_2=\dfrac{20}{100}=0.2\ \mathrm{cm}\)
Step 2: \(P(10\ \mathrm m)=1.01\times10^5+1000(9.8)(10)=1.99\times10^5\ \mathrm{Pa}\)
Step 3: \(P(20\ \mathrm m)=1.01\times10^5+1.96\times10^5=2.97\times10^5\ \mathrm{Pa}\)
Worked derivation: \[W_1=F_1d_1=50(0.20)=10\ \mathrm J=F_2d_2=5000(0.002)\ \Rightarrow\text{energy is conserved}\]
Check: \[\text{gauge pressure doubles }(0.98\to1.96\times10^5\ \mathrm{Pa})\text{, but atmospheric pressure is added to both}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{pressure applied to an enclosed fluid is transmitted undiminished, so the force multiplies by the area ratio, while the distance divides by it; absolute pressure has a constant atmospheric part, so it grows linearly but not proportionally with depth}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{a hydraulic lift multiplies the force; and atmospheric pressure is ignored}\); (B) \(\text{uses a ratio of 10, and pressure does increase with depth}\); (D) \(\text{energy would not be conserved, and pressure is linear in depth}\).
Key point: \(F_2=F_1A_2/A_1,\ d_2=d_1A_1/A_2;\ P=P_a+\rho gh\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Finding the linear expansion coefficient of a brass rod from measured lengths, and deducing the area and volume coefficients
questions.question: A brass rod is 1.0000 m long at 20 °C. When it is heated in a steam jacket to 100 °C, its length is measured as 1.0015 m. What is the coefficient of linear expansion, and what are the approximate coefficients of area and volume expansion? What happens to a circular hole in a brass plate when the plate is heated?
options: A) \(1.5\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm K^{-1}\); area \(3\times10^{-3}\), volume \(4.5\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm K^{-1}\); the hole shrinks
B) \(1.875\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm K^{-1}\); area and volume coefficients equal to it; the hole shrinks
C) \(1.875\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm K^{-1}\); area \(3.75\times10^{-6}\), volume \(5.6\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm K^{-1}\); the hole stays the same size
D) \(1.875\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm K^{-1}\); area about \(3.75\times10^{-5}\) and volume about \(5.6\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm K^{-1}\); the hole becomes larger, as if it were made of brass
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(\alpha=1.875\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm K^{-1}\); \(\beta\approx2\alpha\), \(\gamma\approx3\alpha\); the hole expands.
Given: \(L_0=1.0000\ \mathrm m,\ \Delta L=0.0015\ \mathrm m,\ \Delta T=80\ \mathrm K\)
Formula/Principle: \(\dfrac{\Delta L}{L_0}=\alpha\Delta T;\ \dfrac{\Delta A}{A}=\beta\Delta T\approx2\alpha\Delta T;\ \dfrac{\Delta V}{V}=\gamma\Delta T\approx3\alpha\Delta T\)
Step 1: \(\alpha=\dfrac{0.0015}{1.0000\times80}=1.875\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm K^{-1}\)
Step 2: \(\beta\approx2\alpha=3.75\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm K^{-1};\ \gamma\approx3\alpha\approx5.6\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm K^{-1}\)
Worked derivation: \[A=L^2\Rightarrow A(1+\beta\Delta T)=L_0^2(1+\alpha\Delta T)^2\approx L_0^2(1+2\alpha\Delta T)\ (\text{dropping }(\alpha\Delta T)^2\approx2\times10^{-6})\]
Check: \[1.0000\left[1+1.875\times10^{-5}\times80\right]=1.0015\ \mathrm m\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{every linear dimension of the plate, including the circumference of the hole, grows by the same fraction, so the hole enlarges like a brass disc would}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{forgets to divide by }\Delta T\text{, and the hole grows}\); (B) \(\text{area and volume coefficients are about 2 and 3 times }\alpha\); (C) \(\text{power-of-ten slip, and the hole does change}\).
Key point: \(\alpha=\Delta L/(L_0\Delta T);\ \beta\approx2\alpha,\ \gamma\approx3\alpha;\ \text{holes expand}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Net work and heat in a triangular cycle on a P–V diagram, leg by leg
questions.question: An ideal gas is taken round a cycle A → B → C → A. At A: \(V=1.0\) L, \(P=1.0\times10^5\) Pa; at B: \(V=1.0\) L, \(P=3.0\times10^5\) Pa; at C: \(V=3.0\) L, \(P=1.0\times10^5\) Pa. The path B → C is a straight line on the P–V diagram, and C → A is at constant pressure. What is the net work done by the gas in one cycle, and what is the net heat absorbed?
options: A) 200 J by the gas; 200 J of heat absorbed
B) 400 J by the gas; 400 J absorbed
C) 200 J on the gas; 200 J released
D) Zero work, because the gas returns to its starting state
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Net work 200 J by the gas; net heat 200 J absorbed.
Given: \(A(1.0\ \mathrm L,1.0\times10^5),\ B(1.0\ \mathrm L,3.0\times10^5),\ C(3.0\ \mathrm L,1.0\times10^5)\)
Formula/Principle: \(W=\displaystyle\int P\,dV=\text{area under the path};\ \text{cycle: }\Delta U=0\Rightarrow Q=W\)
Step 1: \(A\to B:\ \Delta V=0\Rightarrow W=0\)
Step 2: \(B\to C:\ W=\tfrac{(3.0+1.0)\times10^5}{2}\times2.0\times10^{-3}=400\ \mathrm J\)
Step 3: \(C\to A:\ W=1.0\times10^5\times(-2.0\times10^{-3})=-200\ \mathrm J;\ W_{net}=200\ \mathrm J\)
Worked derivation: \[W_{net}=\text{area of the triangle}=\tfrac12(2.0\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m^3})(2.0\times10^5\ \mathrm{Pa})=200\ \mathrm J\]
Check: \[\text{with V on the horizontal axis, A}\to\text{B}\to\text{C}\to\text{A is clockwise, so the net work is done by the gas}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{internal energy is a state function, so it returns to its initial value; the first law then requires the net heat absorbed to equal the net work done, which is the enclosed area}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{counts only the expansion leg}\); (C) \(\text{a clockwise cycle does positive work}\); (D) \(\text{returning to the same state makes }\Delta U=0\text{, not W}\).
Key point: \(\text{cyclic process: }Q_{net}=W_{net}=\text{enclosed area (positive if clockwise)}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Molar heat capacities and γ of a mixture of a monatomic and a rigid diatomic gas from equipartition
questions.question: One mole of helium is mixed with one mole of oxygen (treated as a rigid diatomic molecule). Using the law of equipartition of energy, what are the molar \(C_v\), \(C_p\) and \(\gamma\) of the mixture?
options: A) \(C_v=\tfrac32R,\ C_p=\tfrac52R,\ \gamma=\tfrac53\)
D) \(C_v=\tfrac52R,\ C_p=\tfrac72R,\ \gamma=1.4\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(C_v=2R\), \(C_p=3R\), \(\gamma=1.5\).
Given: \(n_{He}=1\ (f=3),\ n_{O_2}=1\ (f=5,\ \text{rigid})\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{equipartition: }\tfrac12k_BT\text{ per degree of freedom}\Rightarrow C_v=\tfrac f2R;\ C_p=C_v+R;\ \text{mixture: }C_v=\dfrac{\sum n_iC_{v,i}}{\sum n_i}\)
Step 1: \(C_v(\mathrm{He})=\tfrac32R,\ C_v(\mathrm{O_2})=\tfrac52R\)
Step 2: \(C_v(\text{mix})=\dfrac{1\cdot\tfrac32R+1\cdot\tfrac52R}{2}=2R\)
Step 3: \(C_p=2R+R=3R;\ \gamma=\dfrac{3R}{2R}=1.5\)
Worked derivation: \[U_{mix}=1\cdot\tfrac32RT+1\cdot\tfrac52RT=4RT\ \text{for 2 mol}\Rightarrow C_v=\frac{1}{2}\frac{dU}{dT}=2R\]
Check: \[\gamma_{He}=1.67>\gamma_{mix}=1.5>\gamma_{O_2}=1.4\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{a monatomic molecule has only 3 translational degrees of freedom, and a rigid diatomic adds 2 rotational ones; the mixture's internal energy is the sum, so its heat capacity per mole is a mole-weighted average}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{these are helium's values alone}\); (B) \(\text{adds the two }C_v\text{ values without dividing by the total moles}\); (D) \(\text{these are oxygen's values alone}\).
Key point: \(C_v=\tfrac f2R;\ \text{mixtures: mole-weighted }C_v;\ \gamma=C_p/C_v\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Reading amplitude and period from the displacement–time graph of a spring–mass oscillator to find k, the maximum speed and the effect of a second spring
questions.question: A 0.50 kg block on a horizontal spring oscillates without friction. Its displacement–time graph is a cosine curve that starts at +5.0 cm at \(t=0\), reaches −5.0 cm at \(t=0.20\) s, and returns to +5.0 cm at \(t=0.40\) s. What are the spring constant and the maximum speed? If a second identical spring is attached in parallel, what is the new period?
options: B) about 123 N/m; about 0.79 m/s; about 0.28 s
C) about 123 N/m; about 0.79 m/s; 0.20 s
D) about 31 N/m; about 1.57 m/s; about 0.57 s
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(k\approx123\) N/m; \(v_{max}\approx0.79\) m/s; new period \(\approx0.28\) s.
Given: \(m=0.50\ \mathrm{kg},\ A=0.050\ \mathrm m,\ T=0.40\ \mathrm s\ (\text{from the graph})\)
Formula/Principle: \(T=2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac mk};\ v_{max}=A\omega;\ \text{parallel springs: }k_p=k_1+k_2\)
Step 1: \(\omega=\dfrac{2\pi}{0.40}=15.7\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}};\ k=m\omega^2=0.50\times246.7\approx123\ \mathrm{N\,m^{-1}}\)
Step 2: \(v_{max}=0.050\times15.7\approx0.79\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\)
Step 3: \(k_p=2k\Rightarrow T'=\dfrac{T}{\sqrt2}=\dfrac{0.40}{1.414}\approx0.28\ \mathrm s\)
Worked derivation: \[x(t)=0.050\cos(15.7t);\ v(t)=-0.785\sin(15.7t);\ |v|\text{ is greatest at }t=0.10\ \mathrm s,\ \text{where }x=0\]
Check: \[2\pi\sqrt{\frac{0.50}{123}}=2\pi(0.0637)\approx0.40\ \mathrm s\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the graph gives the period (one full cycle, 0.40 s) and the amplitude (5.0 cm); the speed is greatest where the curve crosses zero, which is where its slope is steepest}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{power-of-ten slip in k, half the correct maximum speed, and a stiffer system cannot have a longer period}\); (C) \(\text{halves the period instead of dividing by }\sqrt2\); (D) \(\text{uses }T=0.80\ \mathrm s\text{ and misplaces the factors}\).
Key point: \(k=4\pi^2m/T^2;\ v_{max}=A\omega;\ \text{parallel springs: }T\to T/\sqrt2\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Length ratio of an open pipe whose fundamental matches the third harmonic of a closed pipe, and how pipe frequencies scale with temperature
questions.question: The fundamental frequency of an open organ pipe equals the third harmonic of a closed organ pipe. What is the ratio of the length of the open pipe to that of the closed pipe? If the air temperature rises from 27 °C to 127 °C, by what factor do the frequencies of both pipes change (neglect end corrections)?
options: A) \(2:3\); each frequency increases by a factor of about 1.15
B) \(3:2\); each frequency increases by a factor of about 1.33
C) \(1:3\); the frequencies do not change
D) \(2:3\); each frequency increases by a factor of 4.7
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(L_{open}:L_{closed}=2:3\); frequencies rise by \(\sqrt{400/300}\approx1.15\).
Given: \(f_1(\text{open})=f_3(\text{closed});\ T_1=300\ \mathrm K,\ T_2=400\ \mathrm K\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{open pipe: }f_n=\dfrac{nv}{2L};\ \text{closed pipe: }f_n=\dfrac{nv}{4L},\ n\text{ odd};\ v\propto\sqrt T\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{v}{2L_o}=\dfrac{3v}{4L_c}\Rightarrow4L_c=6L_o\Rightarrow\dfrac{L_o}{L_c}=\dfrac23\)
Step 2: \(\dfrac{f_2}{f_1}=\dfrac{v_2}{v_1}=\sqrt{\dfrac{400}{300}}=1.155\)
Worked derivation: \[\text{closed pipe: }L_c=3\cdot\frac{\lambda_3}{4}\ (\text{node at the closed end, antinode at the open end});\ \text{open pipe: }L_o=\frac{\lambda_1}{2};\ \lambda_1=\lambda_3\Rightarrow\frac{L_o}{L_c}=\frac{1/2}{3/4}=\frac23\]
Check: \[L_c=0.75\ \mathrm m,\ L_o=0.50\ \mathrm m,\ v=340:\ f_1(\text{open})=340\ \mathrm{Hz},\ f_3(\text{closed})=\frac{3(340)}{3.0}=340\ \mathrm{Hz}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{equal frequencies in the same air mean equal wavelengths, so the pipe lengths must hold the same wavelength as half a wave and three-quarters of a wave; the speed of sound depends on the absolute temperature}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{inverts the length ratio and uses T instead of }\sqrt T\); (C) \(\text{wrong ratio, and frequency depends on the speed of sound}\); (D) \(\text{uses Celsius temperatures }(127/27)\).
Key point: \(\text{open }f_n=nv/2L\ (\text{all }n);\ \text{closed }f_n=nv/4L\ (\text{odd }n);\ v\propto\sqrt T\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Choosing the graph of the net field along the line joining charges +q and +4q, including where it vanishes
questions.question: Point charges \(+q\) at \(x=0\) and \(+4q\) at \(x=d\) lie on the \(x\)-axis. Which description of the graph of the \(x\)-component of the net electric field \(E_x\) along the axis is correct?
options: A) \(E_x\) is zero at \(x=d/2\) and positive everywhere else
B) \(E_x\) is zero at \(x=2d/3\); it is negative for all \(x<0\) and \(x>d\)
C) \(E_x\) is never zero on the axis

D) Between the charges, \(E_x\) falls from very large positive values near \(x=0\), passes through zero at \(x=d/3\), and becomes very large and negative near \(x=d\); for \(x<0\), \(E_x\) is negative, and for \(x>d\) it is positive, falling towards zero far away
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Zero at \(x=d/3\); positive just right of \(+q\), negative just left of \(+4q\); negative for \(x<0\), positive for \(x>d\).
Given: \(+q\text{ at }0,\ +4q\text{ at }d\)
Formula/Principle: \(E=\dfrac{kq}{r^2}\text{ directed away from a positive charge; superposition}\)
Step 1: \(\text{between the charges: }E_x=\dfrac{kq}{x^2}-\dfrac{4kq}{(d-x)^2}\)
Step 2: \(E_x=0\Rightarrow\dfrac1{x^2}=\dfrac4{(d-x)^2}\Rightarrow d-x=2x\Rightarrow x=\dfrac d3\)
Step 3: \(x<0:\ \text{both fields point in the }-x\text{ direction};\ x>d:\ \text{both point in }+x\)
Worked derivation: \[x=\tfrac d3:\ \frac{kq}{d^2/9}=\frac{9kq}{d^2},\qquad\frac{4kq}{(2d/3)^2}=\frac{4kq}{4d^2/9}=\frac{9kq}{d^2}\ \checkmark\]
Check: \[\text{the null point is closer to the smaller charge, so that its shorter distance compensates for its smaller charge}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{between two like charges, their fields point in opposite directions, so they cancel at one point; outside, they point the same way and never cancel}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{the midpoint is a null only for equal charges, and the field is negative for }x<0\); (B) \(2d/3\text{ is nearer the larger charge, and the field is positive for }x>d\); (C) \(\text{like charges always have a null point between them}\).
Key point: \(\text{like charges: null between them, nearer the smaller charge: }x=d/(1+\sqrt{q_2/q_1})\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: How the potentials of a point charge and of a dipole change with distance and direction
questions.question: An electric dipole has potential \(V_0\) at a point on its axis at distance \(r\) from its centre (\(r\gg\) dipole length). What is the potential on the axis at \(2r\), and at distance \(r\) on the equatorial line? For comparison, how does the potential of a single point charge change when the distance doubles?
options: A) \(V_0/4\) on the axis at \(2r\); zero on the equatorial line; a point charge's potential halves
B) \(V_0/2\) on the axis; \(V_0/2\) on the equatorial line; a point charge's potential falls to a quarter
C) \(V_0/8\) on the axis; \(-V_0\) on the equatorial line; a point charge's potential halves
D) \(V_0/4\) on the axis; \(V_0\) on the equatorial line; a point charge's potential is unchanged
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(V_0/4\); 0; a point charge's potential halves.
Given: \(V_{axis}(r)=V_0;\ r\gg2a\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{dipole: }V=\dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{p\cos\theta}{r^2};\ \text{point charge: }V=\dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac qr\)
Step 1: \(\text{axis }(\theta=0):\ V\propto\dfrac1{r^2}\Rightarrow V(2r)=\dfrac{V_0}{4}\)
Step 2: \(\text{equatorial line }(\theta=90^\circ):\ \cos\theta=0\Rightarrow V=0\)
Step 3: \(\text{point charge: }V\propto\dfrac1r\Rightarrow\text{halves}\)
Worked derivation: \[V_{axis}=\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\left[\frac{q}{r-a}-\frac{q}{r+a}\right]=\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{2qa}{r^2-a^2}\approx\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{p}{r^2}\]
Check: \[\text{equatorial point: equidistant from }+q\text{ and }-q\Rightarrow\frac{kq}{s}-\frac{kq}{s}=0\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the potentials of the two opposite charges nearly cancel far away, leaving a term that falls one power of r faster than for a single charge; on the equatorial line, they cancel exactly}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{uses }1/r\text{ for the dipole, and the equatorial potential is zero}\); (C) \(1/r^3\text{ is the dipole field's dependence, not the potential's}\); (D) \(\text{the equatorial potential is zero, and a point charge's potential depends on r}\).
Key point: \(\text{dipole: }V\propto\cos\theta/r^2\ (0\text{ on the equator});\ \text{point charge: }V\propto1/r\)

questions.sub_topic: Current from four identical cells in series, in parallel and with one cell reversed, and where the chemical energy goes
questions.question: Four identical cells, each of emf 1.5 V and internal resistance 0.50 Ω, are connected to an external resistor of 2.0 Ω. What is the current (a) with all four in series, (b) with all four in parallel, and (c) in series with one cell connected the wrong way round? In case (a), what fraction of the chemical power is delivered to the resistor?
options: A) 3.0 A; 0.75 A; 1.5 A; all of it
B) 1.5 A; 3.0 A; 0 A; one quarter
C) 1.5 A; about 0.71 A; 0.75 A; one half
D) 0.75 A; about 0.71 A; 1.5 A; one half
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 1.5 A; about 0.71 A; 0.75 A; half the chemical power reaches the resistor.
Given: \(E=1.5\ \mathrm V,\ r=0.50\ \Omega,\ R=2.0\ \Omega,\ n=4\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{series: }I=\dfrac{nE}{R+nr};\ \text{parallel: }I=\dfrac{E}{R+r/n};\ \text{power: }EI_{total}=I^2R+I^2r_{total}\)
Step 1: \(\text{(a) }I=\dfrac{6.0}{2.0+2.0}=1.5\ \mathrm A\)
Step 2: \(\text{(b) }I=\dfrac{1.5}{2.0+0.125}\approx0.706\ \mathrm A\)
Step 3: \(\text{(c) net emf}=3(1.5)-1.5=3.0\ \mathrm V,\ \text{internal resistance still }2.0\ \Omega\Rightarrow I=\dfrac{3.0}{4.0}=0.75\ \mathrm A\)
Worked derivation: \[\text{(a) chemical power}=6.0\times1.5=9.0\ \mathrm W;\ I^2R=1.5^2\times2.0=4.5\ \mathrm W;\ I^2(nr)=4.5\ \mathrm W\Rightarrow\text{fraction}=\tfrac12\]
Check: \[\text{Kirchhoff's loop rule in (c): }4.5-1.5=0.75(2.0)+0.75(2.0)=3.0\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the loop rule expresses energy conservation: the net emf around the loop equals the total potential drop; a reversed cell subtracts its emf but still adds its internal resistance. In (a), }R=nr\text{, the condition for maximum power, so half the energy is wasted inside the cells}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{ignores internal resistance in (a), and the parallel and reversed cases are wrong}\); (B) \(\text{parallel cells do not add their emfs, and one reversed cell does not cancel all four}\); (D) \(\text{halves the series current and swaps it with the reversed case}\).
Key point: \(\text{series: }nE/(R+nr);\ \text{parallel: }E/(R+r/n);\ \text{reversed cell: emf subtracts, r still adds}\)
