questions.sub_topic: Torque, net force, equilibrium and potential energy of a current loop in a uniform magnetic field
questions.question: A rectangular coil of \(N\) turns, area \(A\) and current \(I\) is free to turn in a uniform magnetic field \(\vec B\). Its magnetic moment is \(\vec m=NI\vec A\). Which statement is correct?
options: A) The coil experiences a net force along \(\vec B\) as well as a torque, and the torque is greatest when \(\vec m\) is parallel to \(\vec B\)

B) The net force on the coil is zero, and the torque \(\vec\tau=\vec m\times\vec B\) is greatest when the plane of the coil is parallel to \(\vec B\); the coil is in stable equilibrium when \(\vec m\) is parallel to \(\vec B\) and in unstable equilibrium when antiparallel, and turning it from the stable to the unstable position needs work \(2mB\)
C) The torque is zero whatever the orientation, because the forces on opposite sides cancel
D) The coil is in stable equilibrium when \(\vec m\) is antiparallel to \(\vec B\), where its potential energy is lowest
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Zero net force; \(\vec\tau=\vec m\times\vec B\), largest with the coil's plane parallel to \(\vec B\); stable when parallel; work \(2mB\) to reverse.
Given: \(\vec m=NI\vec A,\ \text{uniform }\vec B\)
Formula/Principle: \(\vec\tau=\vec m\times\vec B,\ \tau=mB\sin\theta;\ U=-\vec m\cdot\vec B=-mB\cos\theta\)
Step 1: \(\text{opposite sides carry opposite currents in the same field, so their forces cancel: }\vec F_{net}=0\)
Step 2: \(\tau_{max}=mB\text{ at }\theta=90^\circ\ (\vec m\perp\vec B,\ \text{plane of the coil parallel to }\vec B)\)
Step 3: \(U(0^\circ)=-mB\ (\text{minimum, stable}),\ U(180^\circ)=+mB\ (\text{maximum, unstable})\)
Worked derivation: \[W=U(180^\circ)-U(0^\circ)=mB-(-mB)=2mB;\qquad\tau=NIAB\sin\theta\]
Check: \[\text{a small tilt from }\theta=0\text{ gives a torque back towards }\theta=0\text{ (restoring), but from }\theta=180^\circ\text{ the torque turns it further away}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{in a uniform field, the forces on the two sides form a couple; it rotates the coil until its magnetic moment lines up with the field, like a compass needle}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{there is no net force in a uniform field, and the torque is zero when }\vec m\parallel\vec B\); (C) \(\text{the forces cancel, but they form a couple, which gives a torque}\); (D) \(\text{antiparallel is the position of maximum energy (unstable)}\).
Key point: \(\text{uniform B: }F=0,\ \tau=mB\sin\theta,\ U=-mB\cos\theta\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Choosing the time graph of the displacement current, and of the magnetic field between the plates, while a capacitor charges through a resistor
questions.question: An uncharged 2.0 µF parallel-plate capacitor is connected at \(t=0\) through a 5.0 kΩ resistor to a 10 V battery. Which description of the graph of the displacement current \(i_d\) between the plates against time, and of the magnetic field at a fixed point between the plates (inside the plate area), is correct?
options: A) \(i_d\) is zero at all times, because no charge crosses the gap
B) \(i_d\) rises from zero to a steady 2.0 mA and stays there; the magnetic field between the plates is zero
C) \(i_d\) grows exponentially without limit

D) \(i_d\) starts at 2.0 mA and decays exponentially with time constant 10 ms, equal at every instant to the conduction current in the wires; the magnetic field at the point is proportional to \(i_d\), so it also decays exponentially to zero
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(i_d=2.0\,e^{-t/10\ \mathrm{ms}}\) mA, equal to the conduction current; the field decays the same way.
Given: \(C=2.0\ \mu\mathrm F,\ R=5.0\ \mathrm{k}\Omega,\ V=10\ \mathrm V\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{charging: }I(t)=\dfrac VRe^{-t/RC};\ i_d=\varepsilon_0\dfrac{d\Phi_E}{dt}=\dfrac{dq}{dt};\ \text{Ampere–Maxwell: }\oint\vec B\cdot d\vec l=\mu_0(i_c+i_d)\)
Step 1: \(I(0)=\dfrac{10}{5000}=2.0\ \mathrm{mA};\ \tau=RC=5000\times2.0\times10^{-6}=10\ \mathrm{ms}\)
Step 2: \(\text{between the plates, }\Phi_E=\dfrac{q}{\varepsilon_0}\Rightarrow i_d=\dfrac{dq}{dt}=I(t)\)
Step 3: \(\text{at radius }r\text{ inside plates of radius }R_0:\ B=\dfrac{\mu_0i_dr}{2\pi R_0^2}\propto i_d\)
Worked derivation: \[q(t)=CV\left(1-e^{-t/RC}\right)\Rightarrow\frac{dq}{dt}=\frac{V}{R}e^{-t/RC};\quad i_d(10\ \mathrm{ms})=2.0e^{-1}\approx0.74\ \mathrm{mA}\]
Check: \[\text{as }t\to\infty,\ q\to CV=20\ \mu\mathrm C,\ \text{the field between the plates stops changing, so }i_d\to0\text{ and }B\to0\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the changing electric field between the plates acts as a current that continues the conduction current across the gap, so current is continuous around the circuit and produces a magnetic field there}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{no charge crosses, but the changing electric flux gives a displacement current}\); (B) \(\text{the charging current decays rather than rising, and B is not zero between the plates}\); (C) \(\text{the current is limited by the battery and resistor, and it decays}\).
Key point: \(i_d=\varepsilon_0\,d\Phi_E/dt=\text{conduction current};\ \text{RC charging: both decay as }e^{-t/RC}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Image positions and magnifications for a concave mirror as the object moves from beyond 2f to inside f
questions.question: A concave mirror has a focal length of 15 cm. Where is the image, and what is its magnification, when an object is placed at 20 cm in front of the mirror? Which statement about other positions is also correct?
options: A) 60 cm behind the mirror, virtual, \(m=+3\); an object at 30 cm gives a diminished image

B) 60 cm in front of the mirror, real and inverted, \(m=-3\); an object at 30 cm (centre of curvature) gives a real, inverted image of the same size at 30 cm, an object at 10 cm gives a virtual, erect image magnified 3 times, and an object very far away forms its image at the focus
C) 8.6 cm in front of the mirror, \(m=-0.43\); an object at 10 cm gives a real image
D) 60 cm in front of the mirror, \(m=+3\); an object at the focus forms its image at the centre of curvature
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Real, inverted, at 60 cm in front, \(m=-3\); the other cases are as stated.
Given: \(f=-15\ \mathrm{cm},\ u=-20\ \mathrm{cm}\ (\text{Cartesian sign convention})\)
Formula/Principle: \(\dfrac1v+\dfrac1u=\dfrac1f;\ m=-\dfrac vu\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac1v=-\dfrac1{15}+\dfrac1{20}=\dfrac{-4+3}{60}=-\dfrac1{60}\Rightarrow v=-60\ \mathrm{cm}\)
Step 2: \(m=-\dfrac{-60}{-20}=-3\ (\text{real, inverted, three times larger})\)
Step 3: \(u=-30:\ \tfrac1v=-\tfrac1{15}+\tfrac1{30}=-\tfrac1{30}\Rightarrow v=-30,\ m=-1;\ u=-10:\ \tfrac1v=-\tfrac1{15}+\tfrac1{10}=\tfrac1{30}\Rightarrow v=+30,\ m=+3\)
Worked derivation: \[u\to-\infty:\ \frac1v=\frac1f\Rightarrow v=f;\qquad u=f:\ \frac1v=0\Rightarrow v\to\infty\]
Check: \[\frac{1}{-60}+\frac{1}{-20}=\frac{-1-3}{60}=-\frac{1}{15}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{as the object moves from far away towards F, the real image moves out from F to infinity and grows; inside F, the reflected rays diverge and appear to come from a virtual, erect, magnified image behind the mirror}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{an object beyond F gives a real image, and an object at 2f gives an image of the same size}\); (C) \(\text{adds the reciprocals instead of subtracting, and an object inside F gives a virtual image}\); (D) \(\text{a real image is inverted, and an object at F forms its image at infinity}\).
Key point: \(1/v+1/u=1/f,\ m=-v/u;\ \text{concave mirror: beyond F real and inverted, inside F virtual and erect}\)

questions.sub_topic: Regions of the hydrogen spectral series, the number of lines from n = 4, and the transition that gives the red Hα line
questions.question: Which statement about the hydrogen spectrum is correct?
options: A) The Lyman series (transitions to \(n=1\)) lies in the ultraviolet, the Balmer series (to \(n=2\)) in the visible, and the Paschen series (to \(n=3\)) in the infrared; atoms excited to \(n=4\) can emit 6 different lines as they return to the ground state, and the red Hα line (656 nm) comes from the transition \(3\to2\)
B) The Balmer series lies in the ultraviolet, and its first line comes from \(2\to1\)
C) Atoms excited to \(n=4\) can emit only 3 different lines
D) All the series lie in the visible region, which is why hydrogen looks pink
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Lyman UV, Balmer visible, Paschen IR; 6 lines from \(n=4\); Hα from \(3\to2\).
Given: \(\text{lines from levels up to }n=4\)
Formula/Principle: \(\dfrac1\lambda=R\left(\dfrac1{n_f^2}-\dfrac1{n_i^2}\right);\ \text{number of lines from level }n=\dfrac{n(n-1)}{2}\)
Step 1: \(n=4:\ \dfrac{4\times3}{2}=6\ (4\to3,4\to2,4\to1,3\to2,3\to1,2\to1)\)
Step 2: \(\text{H}\alpha:\ \dfrac1\lambda=1.097\times10^7\left(\dfrac14-\dfrac19\right)=1.524\times10^6\ \mathrm{m^{-1}}\Rightarrow\lambda\approx656\ \mathrm{nm}\)
Worked derivation: \[\text{Lyman }2\to1:\ \lambda=\frac{1}{R(3/4)}\approx122\ \mathrm{nm}\ (\text{UV});\quad\text{Paschen }4\to3:\ \lambda=\frac{1}{R(7/144)}\approx1875\ \mathrm{nm}\ (\text{IR})\]
Check: \[\text{transitions to lower }n_f\text{ involve larger energy gaps, so shorter wavelengths}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the energy levels crowd together as n increases, so jumps down to }n=1\text{ are large (UV), jumps to }n=2\text{ are moderate (visible) and jumps to }n=3\text{ are small (IR)}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{the Balmer series ends on }n=2\text{ and lies in the visible}\); (C) \(\text{six different transitions are possible}\); (D) \(\text{only the Balmer series is in the visible}\).
Key point: \(\text{Lyman UV, Balmer visible, Paschen IR; lines from level n: }n(n-1)/2\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Reading the binding energy per nucleon curve to decide which nuclear reactions release energy
questions.question: On a graph of binding energy per nucleon against mass number, the curve rises steeply from about 1.1 MeV for deuterium (A = 2), reaches a broad maximum of about 8.8 MeV near A = 56 (iron), and falls slowly to about 7.6 MeV for uranium (A = 238). Which conclusion from this graph is correct?
options: A) Energy is released only when iron nuclei are split into smaller nuclei
B) Fusion of two deuterium nuclei absorbs energy, because deuterium has a low binding energy per nucleon
C) Splitting a uranium nucleus into two medium nuclei absorbs energy, because the products are lighter

D) Energy is released both when a heavy nucleus such as uranium splits into two medium nuclei (fission) and when light nuclei such as deuterium and tritium fuse into helium (fusion), because both processes move nucleons towards the peak of the curve, where they are more tightly bound; for example, D + T → ⁴He + n releases about 17.6 MeV
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Both fission of heavy nuclei and fusion of light nuclei release energy.
Given: \(E_{bn}:\ \mathrm{^2H}\approx1.1,\ \mathrm{^{56}Fe}\approx8.8,\ \mathrm{^{238}U}\approx7.6\ \mathrm{MeV}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{energy released}=\text{(total binding energy of products)}-\text{(total binding energy of reactants)}\)
Step 1: \(\text{fission: products near A}\approx120\text{ have }E_{bn}\approx8.5\ \mathrm{MeV}>7.6\ \mathrm{MeV}\Rightarrow\text{energy released}\)
Step 2: \(\text{fusion: }^4\text{He has }E_{bn}\approx7.07\ \mathrm{MeV}\gg1.1\ \mathrm{MeV}\Rightarrow\text{energy released}\)
Worked derivation: \[\mathrm{^2H+{}^3H\to{}^4He+n}:\ Q=4(7.07)-[2(1.11)+3(2.83)]\approx28.3-10.7\approx17.6\ \mathrm{MeV}\]
Check: \[\text{splitting }^{56}\text{Fe would move nucleons away from the peak, so it would absorb energy}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{iron-56 sits at the peak of the curve; any reaction that brings nuclei closer to the peak, from either side, makes the nucleons more tightly bound and releases the difference as energy}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{iron is at the peak, so splitting it costs energy}\); (B) \(\text{fusion of light nuclei moves up the curve and releases energy}\); (C) \(\text{the fission products are more tightly bound, so energy is released}\).
Key point: \(\text{moving towards A}\approx56\text{ releases energy: fission of heavy nuclei, fusion of light ones}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Using dimensional analysis to find how the frequency of a stretched string depends on its length, tension and mass per unit length, and testing it experimentally
questions.question: A student finds experimentally that the fundamental frequency \(f\) of a stretched string depends only on its length \(L\), tension \(T\) and mass per unit length \(\mu\). Using dimensional analysis with \(f=kL^aT^b\mu^c\), what are \(a\), \(b\) and \(c\)? If the tension is doubled and nothing else changes, by what factor does \(f\) change, and can dimensional analysis give \(k\)?
options: A) \(a=1,\ b=-\tfrac12,\ c=\tfrac12\); \(f\) halves; yes
C) \(a=-1,\ b=\tfrac12,\ c=-\tfrac12\); \(f\) increases by \(\sqrt2\); no, \(k\) (which is \(\tfrac12\)) must be found by experiment or theory
D) \(a=-2,\ b=\tfrac12,\ c=\tfrac12\); \(f\) increases by \(\sqrt2\); no
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(f\propto\dfrac1L\sqrt{\dfrac T\mu}\); doubling \(T\) multiplies \(f\) by \(\sqrt2\); \(k\) cannot be found from dimensions.
Given: \([f]=\mathrm T^{-1},\ [L]=\mathrm L,\ [T]=\mathrm{MLT^{-2}},\ [\mu]=\mathrm{ML^{-1}}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{equate the powers of M, L and T on both sides}\)
Step 1: \(\mathrm M:\ b+c=0;\ \mathrm L:\ a+b-c=0;\ \mathrm T:\ -2b=-1\)
Step 2: \(b=\tfrac12,\ c=-\tfrac12,\ a=c-b=-1\)
Step 3: \(f\propto\sqrt T\Rightarrow f'=\sqrt2f\)
Worked derivation: \[\left[L^{-1}T^{1/2}\mu^{-1/2}\right]=\mathrm L^{-1}\left(\mathrm{MLT^{-2}}\right)^{1/2}\left(\mathrm{ML^{-1}}\right)^{-1/2}=\mathrm L^{-1}\mathrm L^{1/2}\mathrm L^{1/2}\mathrm T^{-1}=\mathrm T^{-1}\ \checkmark\]
Check: \[\text{full result }f=\frac{1}{2L}\sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}}:\ k=\tfrac12\text{, a pure number with no dimensions}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{dimensional analysis fixes the exponents when the quantity depends on exactly three independent quantities, but dimensionless constants are invisible to it; the student can test }f\propto\sqrt T\text{ by changing the hanging mass}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{signs of the exponents are reversed}\); (B) \(\text{the time dimension needs }b=\tfrac12\); (D) \(\text{fails the mass balance}\).
Key point: \(f=k\,L^{-1}(T/\mu)^{1/2};\ \text{dimensions give exponents, not constants}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Comparing range, maximum height and time of flight for projectiles launched at 30° and 60° with the same speed
questions.question: Two balls are thrown from level ground with the same speed of 20 m/s, one at \(30^\circ\) and the other at \(60^\circ\) to the horizontal (\(g=9.8\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\), no air resistance). Which comparison is correct?
options: A) Both have the same range, about 35.3 m; their maximum heights are in the ratio \(1:3\) (about 5.1 m and 15.3 m) and their times of flight in the ratio \(1:\sqrt3\) (about 2.0 s and 3.5 s)
B) The \(60^\circ\) ball travels twice as far as the \(30^\circ\) ball
C) Both have the same maximum height, but different ranges
D) Same range; heights in the ratio \(1:\sqrt3\); equal times of flight
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Equal ranges (35.3 m); heights 1 : 3; times 1 : √3.
Given: \(u=20\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}},\ \theta_1=30^\circ,\ \theta_2=60^\circ\)
Formula/Principle: \(R=\dfrac{u^2\sin2\theta}{g},\ H=\dfrac{u^2\sin^2\theta}{2g},\ T_f=\dfrac{2u\sin\theta}{g}\)
Step 1: \(\sin60^\circ=\sin120^\circ\Rightarrow R=\dfrac{400(0.866)}{9.8}\approx35.3\ \mathrm m\text{ for both}\)
Step 2: \(H_{30}=\dfrac{400(0.25)}{19.6}\approx5.1\ \mathrm m,\ H_{60}=\dfrac{400(0.75)}{19.6}\approx15.3\ \mathrm m\)
Step 3: \(T_{30}=\dfrac{2(20)(0.5)}{9.8}\approx2.04\ \mathrm s,\ T_{60}=\dfrac{2(20)(0.866)}{9.8}\approx3.53\ \mathrm s\)
Worked derivation: \[\frac{H_{30}}{H_{60}}=\frac{\sin^230^\circ}{\sin^260^\circ}=\frac{1/4}{3/4}=\frac13;\qquad\frac{T_{30}}{T_{60}}=\frac{\sin30^\circ}{\sin60^\circ}=\frac1{\sqrt3}\]
Check: \[R=u_xT_f:\ 17.32\times2.04\approx35.3\ \mathrm m,\ 10\times3.53\approx35.3\ \mathrm m\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{complementary angles give the same }\sin2\theta\text{, so the same range; the steeper throw goes higher and stays up longer but moves forward more slowly}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{the ranges are equal for complementary angles}\); (C) \(\text{the heights differ, and the ranges are equal}\); (D) \(\text{heights depend on }\sin^2\theta\text{, and the times differ}\).
Key point: \(\theta\text{ and }90^\circ-\theta\text{: same R; }H\propto\sin^2\theta,\ T\propto\sin\theta\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Static friction adjusting to the applied force below the limit, and the acceleration once kinetic friction takes over
questions.question: A 10 kg box rests on a horizontal floor. The coefficients of static and kinetic friction are 0.50 and 0.40 (\(g=9.8\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\)). What is the friction force when a horizontal push of 40 N is applied, and what is the acceleration when the push is 60 N? Which statement about rolling friction is also correct?
options: A) 49 N; 1.1 m/s²; rolling friction is larger than sliding friction
B) 40 N (the box stays at rest); 2.08 m/s²; rolling friction is much smaller than sliding friction, which is why wheels and ball bearings reduce friction
C) 39.2 N; 6.0 m/s²; rolling friction equals kinetic friction
D) 0 N; 2.08 m/s²; rolling friction is zero
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Friction 40 N (no motion); acceleration 2.08 m/s²; rolling friction is much smaller.
Given: \(m=10\ \mathrm{kg},\ \mu_s=0.50,\ \mu_k=0.40,\ N=mg=98\ \mathrm N\)
Formula/Principle: \(f_s\le\mu_sN\ (\text{self-adjusting});\ f_k=\mu_kN;\ F-f_k=ma\)
Step 1: \(f_{s,max}=0.50\times98=49\ \mathrm N;\ 40\ \mathrm N<49\ \mathrm N\Rightarrow\text{no motion, }f_s=40\ \mathrm N\)
Step 2: \(60\ \mathrm N>49\ \mathrm N\Rightarrow\text{box slides};\ f_k=0.40\times98=39.2\ \mathrm N\)
Step 3: \(a=\dfrac{60-39.2}{10}=2.08\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\)
Worked derivation: \[\text{at rest: }\sum F=40-f_s=0\Rightarrow f_s=40\ \mathrm N\ (\text{less than its maximum }49\ \mathrm N)\]
Check: \[\text{a push just above 49 N starts the motion, after which only }39.2\ \mathrm N\text{ opposes it, so the box accelerates}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{static friction only becomes as large as needed to prevent motion, up to }\mu_sN\text{; once sliding, the smaller kinetic friction acts. A rolling body's contact point is momentarily at rest, so there is very little resistance}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{uses the maximum static friction when the push is smaller; rolling friction is smaller}\); (C) \(\text{uses kinetic friction for a box at rest and ignores friction for the acceleration}\); (D) \(\text{static friction cannot be zero when a force is applied, and rolling friction is small but not zero}\).
Key point: \(f_s=F_{applied}\text{ up to }\mu_sN;\ \text{then }f_k=\mu_kN;\ \text{rolling} \ll \text{sliding friction}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Maximum compression of a spring by a block sliding on a rough floor, using the work–energy theorem with a variable spring force and friction
questions.question: A 0.50 kg block slides at 2.0 m/s on a rough horizontal floor (coefficient of kinetic friction 0.20) and hits a light spring of spring constant 200 N/m. What is the maximum compression of the spring (\(g=9.8\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\)), and how is the block's initial kinetic energy shared at that moment?
options: A) 10 cm; all the kinetic energy is stored in the spring
B) 5.0 cm; half is stored and half is lost to friction
C) 20 cm; friction does no work because the floor does not move
D) About 9.5 cm; about 0.91 J is stored in the spring and about 0.09 J is converted to heat by friction
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) About 9.5 cm; ≈ 0.91 J stored, ≈ 0.09 J to friction.
Given: \(m=0.50\ \mathrm{kg},\ v=2.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}},\ \mu_k=0.20,\ k=200\ \mathrm{N\,m^{-1}}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{work–energy theorem: }\Delta K=W_{spring}+W_{friction};\ W_{spring}=-\tfrac12kx^2,\ W_{friction}=-\mu_kmgx\)
Step 1: \(0-\tfrac12(0.50)(2.0)^2=-\tfrac12(200)x^2-0.20(0.50)(9.8)x\)
Step 2: \(100x^2+0.98x-1.0=0\Rightarrow x=\dfrac{-0.98+\sqrt{0.9604+400}}{200}=\dfrac{-0.98+20.024}{200}\approx0.0952\ \mathrm m\)
Step 3: \(\tfrac12kx^2=100(0.0952)^2\approx0.906\ \mathrm J;\ \mu_kmgx=0.98(0.0952)\approx0.093\ \mathrm J\)
Worked derivation: \[W_{spring}=-\int_0^xkx'\,dx'=-\tfrac12kx^2\ (\text{variable force: area under the F–x line});\qquad0.906+0.093\approx1.00\ \mathrm J=K_i\]
Check: \[\text{without friction: }x=v\sqrt{m/k}=2.0\sqrt{0.0025}=0.10\ \mathrm m;\ \text{friction makes the compression slightly smaller}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the spring force grows linearly with compression, so its work is found from the area of a triangle, while friction is constant; together they remove all the kinetic energy}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{ignores friction}\); (B) \(\text{friction takes only about 9 percent, not half}\); (C) \(\text{kinetic friction does negative work on the sliding block, and 20 cm would store 4 J, more than the 1 J available}\).
Key point: \(K_i=\tfrac12kx^2+\mu_kmgx;\ \text{spring work}=\tfrac12kx^2\text{ (variable force)}\)

questions.sub_topic: Choosing the angular velocity and angular momentum graphs when a ring is dropped onto a spinning disc, and the kinetic energy lost
questions.question: A disc with moment of inertia 0.40 kg m² spins freely at 10 rad/s about a vertical axis. At \(t=2.0\) s, a ring of moment of inertia 0.10 kg m² (initially not rotating) is gently placed on it coaxially, and the two soon rotate together. Which description of the graphs of angular momentum and angular velocity against time, and of the energy change, is correct?
options: A) Both the angular momentum and the angular velocity stay constant at their initial values; no energy is lost
B) The angular momentum drops from 4.0 to 3.2 kg m²/s at \(t=2.0\) s; the angular velocity is unchanged

C) The total angular momentum stays constant at 4.0 kg m²/s (a horizontal line); the angular velocity drops from 10 rad/s to 8.0 rad/s around \(t=2.0\) s and then stays constant; the kinetic energy falls from 20 J to 16 J, the 4 J being dissipated by friction between the ring and the disc
D) The angular velocity rises to 12.5 rad/s, because the moment of inertia increases; kinetic energy is conserved
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) L constant at 4.0 kg m²/s; ω falls from 10 to 8.0 rad/s; KE falls from 20 J to 16 J.
Given: \(I_1=0.40\ \mathrm{kg\,m^2},\ \omega_1=10\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}},\ I_2=0.10\ \mathrm{kg\,m^2}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{no external torque about the axis}\Rightarrow L=I\omega\text{ conserved};\ K=\tfrac12I\omega^2=\dfrac{L^2}{2I}\)
Step 1: \(L=0.40\times10=4.0\ \mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-1}}\)
Step 2: \(\omega_f=\dfrac{4.0}{0.40+0.10}=8.0\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}\)
Step 3: \(K_i=\tfrac12(0.40)(10)^2=20\ \mathrm J;\ K_f=\tfrac12(0.50)(8.0)^2=16\ \mathrm J;\ \text{loss}=4\ \mathrm J\)
Worked derivation: \[\frac{K_f}{K_i}=\frac{L^2/2I_f}{L^2/2I_i}=\frac{I_i}{I_f}=\frac{0.40}{0.50}=0.8\]
Check: \[I_f\omega_f=0.50\times8.0=4.0\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{friction between the ring and the disc is internal to the system, so it transfers angular momentum from disc to ring without changing the total, but it does dissipate kinetic energy, as in an inelastic collision}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{the moment of inertia increases, so the angular velocity must fall}\); (B) \(\text{angular momentum is conserved, and the angular velocity changes}\); (D) \(\text{a larger I with the same L gives a smaller angular velocity, and KE is not conserved}\).
Key point: \(\text{no external torque: }I_1\omega_1=(I_1+I_2)\omega_f;\ \text{KE falls by the factor }I_1/(I_1+I_2)\)
